speechtext: THE LATE J. G. MacKAY

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to inform the House of the death of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island, the Hon. J. G. MacKay.
Mr. MacKay had been Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island for just over five years, having been sworn to that office on October 6, 1969. He had been looking forward to release from his responsibilities early in the new year and it is particularly sad that he should not have been able to enjoy the well-earned retirement for which he was undoubtedly planning.
Mr. MacKay had been active in the life and public affairs of Prince Edward Island for many years. He was first elected, by acclamation, to the Legislative Assembly of the province in 1949. He was re-elected four times thereafter. He entered the cabinet of the province as minister without portfolio in 1952 and was minister of public works and highways from 1955 to 1959. In many roles he rendered a distinguished service to the life of the province and the community in which he lived. I am sure all hon. members would wish that the sympathy of this House be extended through you, Mr. Speaker, to Mrs. MacKay and the members of her family.
Hon. members who were here in 1966 at the time of the death of the Hon. Paul Comtois, then Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, may recall that the death of a lieutenant governor in office presents a constitutional problem. There is no provision in the British North America Act under which an administrator may act during a vacancy in the office of lieutenant governor. To permit the operations of government to proceed, it will be necessary to advance the appointment that had been planned for the retirement of Mr. MacKay from his office. I mention this so that members of the House and the public may understand the reasons for what might otherwise appear to be unseemly haste in filling the office that has been left vacant so suddenly.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all four members of parliament from Prince Edward Island when I say that we were all very saddened to learn of the passing of the much beloved representative
of the Queen in our province. In this post, as in his many positions of responsibility throughout a long and exam-plary life, his record is one of cheerful and untiring service.
The late J. George MacKay was a life-long resident of my constituency. I express my sympathy to his many friends and neighbours, whom I have the honour to represent. On their behalf, and on behalf of all Prince Edward Islanders, I wish to extend to his widow and family and to his executive council, our sincere sympathy in their great loss.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party members of parliament, I wish to join in extending our sympathy to Mrs. MacKay and her family on this sad occasion.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, most willingly I make mine the eulogy just voiced by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), who informed us of the untimely death of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island. Very briefly his life can thus be summed up: his lamp has burnt out. He is beginning to see his Creator. I am convinced that he has believed and that now he sees everlastingly.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York-Simcoe asked a series of questions about Olympic coins, one of which I believe was based on an interim report I tabled pointing out the anticipated sales in the amount of $644 million under this project. The hon. gentleman is accurate in stating that the law limits the face value of coins sold to $450 million. The difference between the $450 million and $644 million can be attributed to the increased demand or unexpected demand for premium sets, including the packaging, and the fact that most are being sold at a premium rather than at face value.

subsubtopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO COMMERCIAL BANKS CONCERNING OPERATIONS IN EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister to elaborate in two respects. First of all, he gave an explanation as to the difference between the $600 million some odd figure and the $450 million face value. I should like him to relate that to the report that is already in hand which indicates there is only a 5 per cent premium mark-up on the coins sold to March 31 of this year compared with a 43 per cent mark-up in the projected figures. The second and most interesting point on which I should like him to comment is this, has he in fact satisfied himself that there has been no commission, discount or other advantage paid by COJO or anybody else in respect of the sale of the coinage to the distributors?

subsubtopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO COMMERCIAL BANKS CONCERNING OPERATIONS IN EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, COJO has nothing to do with this program. I can assure the House that there is absolutely no distributor, no outlet, no chartered bank and no individual who is able to obtain Olympic coins at any discount whatever from face value. The private distributors, the people around the world who specialize in coins, do get a discount between the selling price and the $5 value coin. subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-15, respecting oil and gas in Indian lands, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the House was advised in the Speech from the Throne that the government intended to introduce legislation respecting oil and gas on Indian lands. Bill C-15 was given first reading before this House on October 7. It is my pleasure, as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to bring the bill forward for second reading today.
It is a bill which merits the support of all members. All of us are aware of the recent turmoil in oil and gas prices, markets and distribution. All of us are aware how essential it is for Indian bands and people to participate fully in the Canadian economy, getting all the benefits they can from the lands set aside on their behalf. This bill is

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
intended to ensure that equitable benefits from oil and gas production on Indian lands go to the Indian people.
Let me give the House a brief history of oil and gas production on Indian lands so that I may demonstrate how important this legislation is to a great many Indian people-important as a tangible indication that the people of Canada are determined that Indians shall receive the fullest benefits from the resources on their reserves. Most of the wells now producing on Indian lands were drilled between 1947 and 1956. Exploration, drilling and production were governed by regulations under the Indian Act. They were structured to conform closely to Alberta's regulations, for it was in Alberta that the major oil finds were made. They adopted the Alberta model of low royalty rates and long-term leases of 10 and 21 years. Under this plan, the bands received cash bonuses, royalties on actual production, nominal acreage rentals and compensation for surface rights.
This worked well over the years when the oil industry was relatively stable, and it fitted into the oil and gas environment where the wells were located. The need for change was made clear last year when the oil crisis erupted and it became apparent that the regulations of 1966 were not flexible enough to meet the situation. Difficulties arose when it became necessary to consider revising the regulations and it became apparent that the Indian Act was not a sound basis for applying the kind of controls and flexible approach which the situation demanded. It was agreed that new legislation was necessary to make certain that the regulation of this important resource was consistent with the best interests of the Indian bands concerned. The leases entered into under existing regulations called for royalty rates which were not consistent with the new situation, and these rates were locked into those leases. The royalties were determined by agreements which did not-indeed, could not have foreseen the changing times.
It is evident that this inflexible situation requires action and that only legislation will serve the Indian needs. It is essential that the royalties be adjustable without delay when circumstances in the industry change, it is imperative that Indian bands receive royalties which the latest market situation warrants, just as others do. Oil and gas resources on Indian lands cannot be allowed to provide windfall benefits for those operators fortunate enough to have their production coming from Indian reserves. All the oil producing provinces have enacted legislation to amend royalty scales as well as to establish elaborate marketing and production controls of various kinds. Indian bands alone are caught in a situation where regulations cannot be quickly adjusted to the new turn of events.
Fortunately, a study team had been appointed before any oil crisis was visualized. The team included the solicitor for the producing bands, the solicitor for the Alberta Indian Association, and experts in the oil and gas field. The study team worked fast. On March 28, 1974, an order in council set new rates of royalty and established the principle of variable royalties so that rates could be altered to rqeet changing conditions. This was an interim measure. The present bill was drafted to follow up the

provisional changes made by the order in council and to establish the framework needed. It is too bad it could not have been introduced and passed-for I am sure it will be passed quite quickly-before prorogation. However, that was not to be, and the next best thing is the early introduction of the bill which I am presenting today.
Bill C-15 provides a framework for the future regulation of oil and gas activities on Indian lands in the best interests of the bands. Dealing as it does with this one resource, Bill C-15 in no way conflicts with the government's commitment not to amend the Indian Act until the Indian people's proposals are put before the government, the House and the Canadian people. Far from conflicting with the principles of the Indian Act, the bill provides solid benefits to Indian people. Let me summarize its objectives: It reiterates the principles set out in order in council PC 1974-732 which increased royalty rates significantly. It elaborates the scope of the authority contained now in the Indian oil and gas regulation. It set aside the royalty provisions of the existing oil and gas contracts and provides for royalties to be prescribed from time to time by order in council, thus giving the flexibility needed in an ever-changing situation. It enables the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, after first getting the approval of the band concerned, to enter into special arrangements for reducing royalties where conditions warrant that step. It provides that all oil and gas rights granted on Indian reserves may be subject to legislation which is suited to the industry conditions of the day.
In early 1974 there were consultations with the Indian bands about proposed changes in the regulations. The more important proposals concerning royalties have been brought into effect through amendments to regulations. This bill ensures that in the future the regulations will be more flexible and responsive. This bill is concerned mostly with the future. The oil and gas resource is a "once only" proposition. Once the oil is removed from the ground, it will not again enrich the band. Oil and gas production is a relatively shortlived proposition. The Pigeon Lake Indian reserve has oil which was estimated in 1969 to be good for 30 years production at the then prevailing rate. Today, five years later, it is thought these reserves will decline drastically in the next three years due to increased production. The greatest possible return must flow to the band when the oil is taken from the ground and is lost to them forever.
Indian bands will receive, in royalties, about $40 million this year from this important resource. Last year they received $9 million. As oil and gas production declines, there may be a reduction in this income, although with prices being the way they are, no one can tell for certain what the future will bring. Royalty income is based on production and the current selling price of conventional oil and gas. Several reserves are known to be underlain by many millions of barrels of very heavy crude oil. When technology improves, and the price is right, we can expect to see royalty income from this resource flowing into band funds. The bill before us anticipates the day when that happens, for such a particular resource will require flexible approaches, being different in many ways from what is produced today.
October 21, 1974

The bands which enjoy oil revenues will certainly make as good use of the money in the future as they have in the past. Many hon. members-especially those from Alberta-know, for example, how the Enoch, Sawridge and Hobbema bands have improved their communities in economic, cultural and social terms with the benefits of oil income. Others have done the same.
Canadians generally will, I am sure, want to see the Indian people enjoy whatever benefits they can from the reserves set aside on their behalf. Oil and gas were not foreseen in Alberta when the Indian reserves were set aside. They are an accident of time and circumstances. For a people who have generally suffered through the accidents of time and have repeatedly lost their struggles with circumstances, it is an important principle that this bill sets out. The principle is that parliament will do its best to see that the Indian people get the greatest possible benefits from the resources set aside on their behalf. The government believes this bill is important to the Indian people and hopes the House will support it in that view.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not thought to commence my debating in this House with this particular bill. I say that, not because I am not interested in it; there are, in fact, Indian bands and Indian people in my constituency and the area that I know so well who are interested in this bill and in the proceeds and royalties derived from petroleum wells that have been drilled. However, some of the most concerned people in our party are not here today because they did not expect the legislative program to proceed as rapidly as it has.
Indian Affairs
This is probably an indication of the extent to which-he was different in his role as Secretary of State for External Affairs-the present government House leader (Mr. Sharp) has been made more mellow and his task smoother so that it has become, in the best political sense of the word, even more slippery so far as the conduct of House business is concerned. Perhaps the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), the former House leader, may derive the same benefit. Who knows, even the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), at one time House leader, might become a good House leader if he has experience in external affairs.
I am glad to speak following the minister, whom I wish well in the responsibilities that he has assumed. His is one of the most difficult tasks facing any government. We in this country have to come to grips with the problems of the Indian people. I do not say "the Indian problem" because I think there are a number of Indians who have problems, as there are a number of white people and non-Indians who have problems. But the Indian question is a difficult one, as all of us who were here for the opening of parliament are aware. We know what could happen and we know the dangers inherent in the relationship between the government of Canada and the Indian people. But knowing the minister, I think he will do his very best. He had the advantage of getting his start in the city of Edmonton, in the province of Alberta, and he has not been in the east long enough to have all of those good qualities buried under the weight of eastern problems which we all see from time to time.
We must look pretty carefully at this bill, for it is not quite as simple as the minister indicated. In the first place, it is probably the forerunner of other matters that will arise in the future. I am not going to go into them. There is the Mackenzie Valley pipeline and the rights of the Indian people there in connection with petroleum reserves. In addition, the Indian people face many other problems with which the government of Canada will have to contend. I think it has to contend with them on the basis that the long period of wardship, of trusteeship, must now come to an end and the Indian people must be deemed to be qualified to deal with their problems as they see fit. This does not mean that they will not make mistakes, as we have made mistakes in the past. But if they are not given the opportunity to find their own methods of dealing with their difficulties, then they will stay as our wards for a long time-a situation that is undesirable both for them and for us.
Although what I now say is probably a little irrelevant, it is nevertheless related to this whole question. Just a few days ago I had the pleasure of accompanying the new Lieutenant-Governor of Alberta, Ralph Steinhauer, himself a full-blooded Indian, into the Rainbow Lake area in the Assumption district where there is a band of Slavey Indians who have petroleum reserves in respect of which the government has been receiving royalties from time to time. On my visit there I met with people I have known for 15 to 20 years, such as Chief Harry Chonkolay, his wife Elizabeth, and many others. Some I met for the first time almost 40 years ago when I went into Fort Vermillion country. At that time we went by boat. There were no roads, railway or aircraft and so I walked 30 to 40 miles into the area and first met some of these people.

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
They have done a pretty fair job of trying to conduct the affairs of their band. They have had problems with the department and also with the white people who have gone into the area, but generally the chiefs and the band councils have brought the affairs of their people along with a moderate degree of success. In speaking to the chief at the banquet given for His Honour, I learned of the difficulties facing them. He told me, "We are older; we are getting on in years. We have managed the affairs of our people, with their consent, as their elected representatives, and have negotiated with the government for many years. But it is time to yield our place to young men and women and let them manage the affairs of the band instead of us".
Their complaint was that as they looked around and talked to the young people, they were told, "We do not want the job. The government of Canada and the representatives of the Indian Affairs department have not over the years conducted themselves in a way that lends itself to a reasonable arrangement being arrived at between our people and the rest of the people of Canada so that in due course the Indian people can, if they see fit, take their place with the other people of Canada or, if they see fit, stay on the reserve". These people read about and watched on television the violence at Kenora, British Columbia, and in Ottawa. In light of this, these young people are most reluctant to take upon themselves the responsibility of acting in the band councils, in the councils of the Indian people, and of carrying on in the same way as did their parents, not wanting to use methods of violence, anger and hatred, but of reason, compromise, understanding and co-operation.
This bill might well be an indication of the government's intentions regarding the Indian people. We may be able to go back to the Indian people and tell them that the government has changed, that it is prepared to negotiate with the Indians and give them responsibility for conducting their own affairs. We may be able to say, "We ask you, the young people, to take your place in the councils of your own people and to conduct affairs for them". For this reason I attach a great deal of importance to this legislation.
I am confident there will be other bills to follow. There is even talk about a complete revision of the Indian Act. One young gentleman who has been prominent for some years in the councils of native people in my province-he was originally from my constituency-namely, Harold Cardinal, has with the aid of Indian councils taken it upon himself to provide a model Indian Act. He was here with it not long ago at the time of discussions with the minister and his colleagues.
I use that fact to illustrate that many of these young people are competent, knowledgeable and capable of taking their place as representatives of the Indian peoples. They are still suspicious of the extent to which the federal government and the federal department, with a long and sad history of colonialism which I hope has now ended, are prepared to accept them in a relationship which will vest in them the right, at long last, to handle their own affairs. For that reason, while we shall not oppose the passage of this bill, we follow that course dubitatio; we go along with it, but we are a little doubtful. We will use the opportunity

in committee to examine in close detail some of the reasons, consequences and factors which relate to the application of this legislation.
For the reasons I have mentioned, I would refer the minister to clause 3 of the bill. I do not intend to go into the bill in great detail, as that will be done in committee, but to illustrate the point I am trying to make it is essential to refer to the legislation in that we are dealing with its principles. The bill purports to seek ratification and confirmation by this House of certain regulations purported to have been enacted by the governor in council under the Indian oil and gas regulations passed pursuant to section 57 of the act. At first blush, many of us wonder why it is essential, if these regulations have in fact the force of law, having legally been passed and lying squarely within the competence of the governor in council, to come to this House asking parliament to ratify and confirm regulations which to all intents and purposes have the effect of law. I hope the minister will respond to this question, if not when he sums up, then certainly at the committee when he makes his opening statement.
Most of us have been around here long enough to know very well the extent to which this government in particular, and most governments, provincial as well as federal, have steadily eroded the right of parliament to legislate. We know the extent to which governments have taken unto themselves, by almost every bill which is passed, more powers to legislate by order in council, thereby encroaching steadily upon the rights of the representatives of the people. I do not see any great rush by this government or this department to come to parliament and say that, because it passed regulations six months or a year ago, it now thinks it is essential to come back to this high court of parliament for ratification and confirmation. This is the first question the minister will have to answer.
We will want to examine precisely what the government has done, what operations it has carried out and what contractual arrangements it has entered into pursuant to these regulations, to ensure that they are in fact proper, legal and beneficial to the people for whose purposes they are alleged to have been passed. That is primarily a duty and a responsibility of the committee which will be dealing with this subject.
Clause 4 of the bill establishes the point I am making. It provides that the governor in council may make regulations. This is the regulatory granting of power which this House is being asked to approve, and it is enormous in extent. At this point in time in our relations with the Indian people, I am wondering if we can reflect to some extent our desire to limit some of these powers, rather than giving them to the governor in council without inhibition. Can we not reflect our desire to bring in the Indian people and their band councils who, I trust, will be the beneficiaries of the regulations to be passed?
I will not be a member of the committee and will not have the opportunity or the privilege of participating in the discussion, so I throw out these suggestions in the hope that some of my colleagues who will be members will give them thought. For example, the bill provides that the governor in council may make regulations respecting the granting of leases, permits and licences for the exploitation of oil and gas, as well as the terms and conditions
October 21, 1974

thereof. I should like to see inserted in that clause-and of course we cannot do it here-wording to the effect that the governor in council may, after consultation with the Indians and their band councils, make certain regulations.
In respect of the granting of leases, permits and licences, is there any reason why this right cannot be vested in the band councils themselves? Perhaps there is a reason. If there is, I hope the minister will point it out to the committee. The reason may relate to the intention of the government in respect of the proceeds of these royalties, and in this regard I think there is an onus and a responsibility on the government to spell it out. These people have been wards of the government for a hundred years. Surely they should now be allowed to assume responsibility for and to deal with their own affairs, making their own mistakes even as we have done. Why should we not allow the Indian people or band councils to make or grant leases, permits and licences for the exploitation of oil and ga^ on Indian lands? As I understand it, these band councils, through a proper democratic process, have been duly elected to carry out the responsibilities of the Indian people, subject to pressures, even as we are in this House, from the people who elected them. The same argument would apply to the clause dealing with the disposition of any interest in Indian lands necessarily incidental to the exploitation of oil and gas. Why should not the native people and the band councils be the ones, rather than the governor in council, to make these dispositions?
I will not go into the subsequent clause in detail because I think the wording speaks for itself. It refers to regulations providing for the seizure and forfeiture of any oil or gas taken in contravention of any regulations. I think this is an area in which the governor in council should operate. However, I think the wording should make it clear that the governor in council shall seek the consent of the band councils and Indian people affected. That is the case I am trying to make, and I again suggest that the minister and the government respond by pointing out the reason this step should not be taken at this point in the history of the relations of the Canadian government with our Indian people.
In clause 5 there is a principle which I do not like. It may be explained by the minister in the committee. However, it provides that the oil and gas obtained from Indian lands after the coming into force of this legislation is subject to the payment to Her Majesty in right of Canada of the royalties prescribed from time to time by the regulations. This raises the entire question. The minister attempted to go some distance along the road by giving an indication of what these royalties should be. My party, and I am sure many of the Indian people, would be interested in knowing, through the form of a complete and detailed statement, what royalties have been secured and what payments have been made to the government, which I hope the government has held exclusively in trust for the affected Indian bands and band councils.
We would also like to know the extent to which these payments have been diminished with regard to royalties paid to the provincial governments because of changes in the price of petroleum products over the last few months. I do not blame the minister for this. However, I have in
Indian Affairs
mind the situation which prevailed in this country, starting almost a year ago, when we came up against the so-called petroleum problems, the shortages and the doubts which existed in the minds of so many people in other countries as to whether there would be enough petroleum, oil and gas for the western countries. I also have in mind the escalation of price which followed. I would have thought, therefore, the minister would have told us how much money has been lost, if any, to the Indian people because the amounts paid in respect of royalties were substantially less than the amounts paid the provincial government.
Having in mind the increased prices, have the Indian people suffered a substantial loss and, if so, do they have an action for damages against the federal government? It is not necessary for one to be a lawyer to know that if one has a trustee to whom he gives certain rights, through power of attorney, to do things on his behalf, and the trustee acts negligently or foolishly resulting in a substantial loss of money, there may well be a perfectly valid action for damages against the trustee. I know it is not easy to sue the federal government or to tackle city hall. I am not in any sense accusing the minister of misleading the House, but I wonder whether this may be one reason for the clause I referred to earlier. Could there be a potential action against the federal government, and could the effect of this legislation be to vindicate the federal government in what it proposes to do under the regulations? That may have been the intention.
I practised law long enough, before I was induced to enter politics, to know that what governments do is not always right. I have had some measure of success even in suing the federal government, because the federal government sometimes legislates in haste, without due regard for the law and therefore sometimes leaves itself open to legal action. This might very well be the effect of the passage of some of the regulations the government is now asking parliament to ratify.
The minister should realize he is being given notice that the committee will press him closely on this issue as well as on the other issues I have mentioned. That is all I intend to say now, Mr. Speaker. I hope the minister understands that our party will let this bill go to committee. Some of my colleagues may want to make a contribution to this debate. They have knowledge of the issues and may wish to make some comments. However, it is our hope that the bill will in fact receive second reading and go to the committee. I believe I am entitled to express a final caveat to the effect that the minister may expect the closest scrutiny and questioning in the committee. In fact, it will be a great start to his ministerial career.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the last speaker, I do not come from a constituency in which there are very many native people, but I do not think that is a reason for not participating in this debate. I believe the welfare of our native people should be the concern of every Canadian.
I should like to commend the minister for his approach to this whole task. I express once again my earnest hope that during this parliament a substantial advance may be made toward giving the native people the measure of justice of which they have been deprived in the past. I do

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
not for a moment doubt the good intentions of the minister in bringing forward this particular legislation. He explained it is for the benefit of the native people in that they may receive a greater share of the royalties. No one could carp or quibble about that good intention. Unfortunately, however, we need more than merely good intentions.
I find this bill to be very sweeping in its provisions. I agree with much that has been said by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). There are few subjects more sensitive and important than the whole question of Indian lands, including mineral rights and gas and oil royalties. It is not only a sensitive, but also a highly complex subject. Before parliament takes the responsibility of passing this legislation, in my judgment there should be the most searching scrutiny.
In this bill I think I see traces of what I regard as paternalism on the part of the department, through the power of regulation, in respect of the control of these matters. I want to see a greater indication that the Indians themselves will be given a measure of management and control over their resources. We want there to be full consultation. I had a short conversation with the minister. I understand that before the government drafted this bill a study team, including the solicitor for the producing bands and the solicitor for the Alberta Indian Association, made some recommendations. I wonder whether such consultation is wide enough. Having been a solicitor myself, I know how busy solicitors are and how apt they are to keep these things to themselves. It seems to me full consultation means a little more than merely telling a few lawyers what this is all about and asking for their comments or recommendations. I wonder whether full consultation has taken place, because this matter affects not only the Indians in Alberta but a whole complex situation which stretches across Canada.
The hon. member for Peace River pointed out that clause 3 of the bill provides that certain regulations which are not specified or described-the minister did not tell us what was in them-are to continue as though they had been passed by parliament. But parliament has not passed them, Mr. Speaker. Parliament has not even seen them. I do not think we should agree to the proposition that something has been done by an act of parliament when such is not the case. Of course, in committee we can find out what the regulations are. I understand that most are designed for the protection of the native people and some are designed to give a measure of control to Indian bands. I do not want to go into the long unhappy history of our dealings with the native people, but I do want to know exactly what the regulations are. Should they not be subject to full consultation and the undertakings which I understand were given by the minister or his predecessors, namely, that no change would be made to the Indian Act without such consultation?
I understand that various groups of Indians across Canada are studying these matters with the assistance of scholars and researchers. One might wonder how we have reached this stage without consultation. Although the regulations are to provide protection for the Indians, they are only part of the legislation, so far as I can make out,

until revoked by the governor in council. If we have something that is protection for our native people, why should it be subject to change overnight? That is a question I should like answered if I were an Indian. I am not suggesting the minister would reduce that protection; I am just giving my opinion that the wording of the bill gives rise to reasonable suspicion.
I agree with the hon. member for Peace River also, that clause 4 gives the widest possible scope to the making of regulations. This, again, hands the whole subject over- without a hint that anybody is to be consulted-to control by the regulations. Everybody knows that the regulations are prepared in the department, and this bill continues that sort of control. It is interesting that only one clause refers to the band council. Clause 5(2) reads;
The minister may, with the approval of the council of the band concerned, enter into a special agreement with any person for a reduction of royalties payable under subsection (1).
I thought the main purpose of the legislation was to increase the amount of royalties payable, not to reduce it. This is the only clause which contains specific reference to the approval of the band council. As the hon. member for Peace River asked, why is approval of the band council not incorporated into the other clauses dealing with what is basically the property of the Indians themselves? Clause 5(1) ends with these words:
-payment to Her Majesty in right of Canada of the royalties prescribed from time to time by the regulations.
There is not a hint there of anything to be held by the Crown in trust for the Indian people. If that is the intention, why not say so and give an assurance to the Indian people that they will benefit? As beneficiaries, they can then assert certain rights which in my judgment they justly claim. The whole bill seems to ignore the sensitivities of the Indians, Mr. Speaker, and I think it must be changed in committee to make certain matters explicit. Let us make it clear that the royalties are there to be used. I can understand that in certain circumstances they should not be paid directly to the Indian bands concerned, but to the federal authorities. However, that principle should be made clear.
The bill is vague in other respects, Mr. Speaker. It has been asked how it fits in with the federal-provincial transfer act of 1930 which I understand applies in the prairie provinces and, in the eyes of the Indians, confers upon them certain explicit rights in respect of gas and oil. When they see this bill, containing power to do almost anything, will they not consider some of those rights lost to them? Such questions can be answered in committee to some extent, but I think they should also be made clear to parliament.
I would urge the government to seek a wide cross-section of Indian opinion before a bill so vital to their interests is made law. This party will be glad to co-operate in any way we can. It is important that, even with the best intentions, we do not add to the suspicion and feeling of paternalism created by such legislation. Sometimes the Indians feel they are kept out of the process of making basic decisions. I believe it is the minister's intention-it certainly is ours-to get away from the era of paternalism and dependence so that our native people can decide questions for themselves.

We have a new minister, and perhaps now is time for him to point out to his officers just what he wants. He should ask that the act be redrawn to ensure that Indians and their band councils are consulted and their right to the royalties held in trust for them is stated in the legislation. He should ensure, with regard to the section which purports to provide that these regulations-which parliament has not even seen-are to have the total force of legislation passed by parliament, that parliament is fully informed of the intent of the regulations and that the Indian people know exactly the effect upon them of the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about Bill C-15, an act respecting oil and gas in Indian lands.
This bill concerns me somewhat since there is an Indian reservation in my constituency following the troubles in the province of Quebec concerning James Bay, I think that the presentation of this bill is giving rise to some apprehension. I have always urged that the Indians be treated with equality and justice in Canada. Since my election to Parliament, when I look at some of the bills brought forward and at the role of the administration in some fields, I become even more apprehensive, Mr. Speaker. We keep saying that we should give back to the Indians their power of administration since we feel they are mature enough to administer themselves. This is what I believe, Mr. Speaker, but this is not what happens actually. I see a striking example of this situation every day in my constituency when I see the manager who is a white man administer the reservation as if it were his own. When he thinks that an Indian can injure or become as educated as he is, because some Indians are educated, he quickly drives him out of the reservation. I say "drive" because he is given a job 200 or 300 miles from the reservation at double or triple the salary he would get on the reservation to prevent him from influencing his people.
As for the others, the government hires them so that they cannot say anything about the administration of the reservation. In this way, the white men take advantage of the Indians on our reservations, and we accept this and think that it is a good thing. Nobody says anything, but the Indians keep protesting to no avail.
That is why I am warning the minister. I know he is still full of good intentions. Today, he brings forth a small bill, but I believe that small bill of a few pages will stir up a big discussion. With regard to the discussion that will and must follow, I am sure the minister will consult the chiefs of the Indian bands because legislation is being passed which concerns their lands.
Indeed, clause 4 says this:
The Governor in Council may make regulations
(a) respecting the granting of leases, permits and licences for the
exploitation of oil and gas in Indian lands and the terms and
conditions thereof;
The governor general "may". Therefore, he has the right to do so. I will not go as far as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and say that the band chiefs should give out those permits and licenses, because the govern-
Indian Affairs
ment must retain authority in Canada, but he must exercise it democratically. It is not enough to merely say that the advice of the Indians authorities will perhaps be sought, that they will be consulted. Indeed, let us have worthwhile discussion with them, let us be sincere with those people as we should be with all Canadians.
I heard it said a while ago that the Indians were somewhat apprehensive whenever the provincial or federal governments were introducing bills such as this one. If I were an Indian myself, I would be justified in being apprehensive. Knowing how many times they have been taken in, I believe I would be concerned myself. That is why I am asking the Minister to be very cautious, to be extremely careful and to try for once, with his bill, to do justice to all Canadians including our native people, with the respect to our neatural resources, with respect to the expropriation of sections of their lands so that we will not have to use public funds, as was done concerning the James Bay project, to give those groups a chance to be heard in our courts.
Mr. Speaker, even if this bill does not amount to very much, I hope that when it is considered on third reading the minister will supply more information on it, which will enable us to vote in a more intelligent way, because the object of today's vote is to refer this bill to the committee for examination.
Actually, we do not accept the principle of this bill. We must provide for an agreement which is absolutely necessary if we want to undertake the development of natural gas deposits and the exploration of new oil reserves, because it will be absolutely necessary then to go through Canadian territory. But this should be done in all fairness and the owners considered as equals and given whatever they are entitled to.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) upon his appointment. I am sure he recognizes, as do other members of the House, that he has accepted an important challenge on behalf of the people of Canada. What will happen with regard to Indian affairs in the next couple of decades will be most important to our country, as I am sure he is well aware. We hope that the minister's work will prove fruitful and will enable our Indian people to be integrated into the mainstream of Canadian life.
I shall preface my remarks by saying that the government has introduced this bill with good intentions. I commend them for that and for other good pieces of legislation of this kind. Our concerns regarding this bill have been referred to by previous speakers. I shall mention only one or two major issues. I am concerned about how extensively the Indian people will become involved in Canadian life as a result of this legislation.
It seems to me that for too long the government has played the role of foster parent to the Indian people, a role in which the Indian people have been subservient to government. I believe this bill intends to give them a better deal for their oil and gas royalties. Nevertheless, from my reading of the bill it is apparent that the government will decide the rate of royalty, when and where development

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
will take place, and so on. Consequently, the Indian people will still be left out of an important process, that of decision-making. If they are to fit fully into the mainstream of Canadian life, we must recognize that these people must participate more fully in decisions affecting their own lives. We can say this for sure: if there is one thing that must become an increasing part of government, it is to begin to think less and less about the rights of specific groups of people and to think more and more about the broader context of human rights. We see this bill brought forward again within the framework of some kind of "Indian" context. If we viewed it simply from a "people's" context, we would see that the need for putting these people into a greater decision-making role would then be necessary and brought forward.
We are about to enter into a period of increasing ferment among the Indian people. I believe we are going to enter into that period of time because those people in any society who are the most suppressed are simply not in the position to agitate or create ferment. It is only when you come close to breaking into the mainstream of life that real agitation and "boiling-over" of a society begins to take place. I am very suspicious that at this time in history we are about to enter into a period when the Indian people, because they have developed significant leadership within their own groups, are going to want more and more of the action. The problem is that we in this country have a very long tradition of government making the decisions for them.
I see the bill and this legislation as another example of the Indian people being promised greater benefits. That sounds good. However, they are not really being told that we are granting to them the privilege of making those decisions. That is what will resist a real upheaval; the granting of greater and greater degrees of responsibility to the Indian people. This bill looks as though we are saying to them, "This is the way we are going to do it today because it is the way we did it yesterday." This seems all right in the close context. However, if we extend it long enough, it in effect says, "We are going to do it this way because it is the way we did it 100 years ago". That is where the danger lies.
Indian people all across Canada have shown a great deal of leadership in the last decade. This should move the government to respond by extending to them a far greater degree of responsibility than is displayed in this bill. I would say essentially what is at hand is the question of self-concept. That is not a quality that anyone gives to someone else. It is something that people develop from doing. It is something that grows out of oneself when one feels he is worth something.
This is another bill in which the government says, "Let us make the decisions because we are going to make good ones." I feel very good about the intent of what they want to do. However, I am rather concerned that the real issue here in the development of the whole Indian society requires that they become a people who have pride in themselves. This means they have to accept a full degree of responsibility in the development of their resources and have more to say about the extent of the royalties and when the resources will be developed. When this bill goes

to committee, and before it comes back for third reading, what ought to be considered is a much more extensive degree of involvement on behalf of the Indian people, in terms of the development of these resources. These comments are essentially singular to that point. While I agree with other speakers who preceeded me, my singular point is that this legislation, in its intent, is good.
When it goes to committee, it needs to be broadened in respect of guaranteeing to the Indian people that they will not only receive greater financial benefits from the government, but they will be guaranteed by government a much higher degree of participation. They must be guaranteed that government will be even more subsidiary to the native people's decisions, than the reverse. Even though it might grant them more financial gain, it will not give them the kind of psychological gain that is, at this period in history, the most important of all considerations.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the sending of this bill to committee. However, a number of comments have been made, and I want to make more, that ought to be made here and borne in mind in committee when the bill is sent there for consideration.
I find all amending legislation confusing. You get a bit of a thing which refers back to the main bill and then to orders in council. You have to assemble all the bits and pieces in order to create a whole piece on which to base any comment. I did that this morning. I scurried around. Thank goodness there is such a thing as a photocopying machine, because I was able to gather together all the various orders in council referred to here. I was then chased back to earlier orders in council, which I managed to find. That referred me back to the Indian Act. I managed to get the relevant sections of that act. I have them in front of me. It has turned out to be a very confusing assemblage of documents.
Even the Indian Act is seated on more complicated documents than just an act of parliament. It goes back to the incorporation of the provinces in confederation. In each of the incorporation acts of the provinces there is a provision covering Indian lands. They are not all the same. We have a great collection of documents that somehow or another we are expected to digest and deal with in six clauses in this brief bill and come to a resolution. I do not believe it is fair to the Indian people, who will be the main beneficiaries under this bill, that we do things in this way. If it is confusing to me, when I have all the facilities of this House at my disposal, to gather together these documents. How much more confusing is it to the Indians who are not here but are watching and will be following the debate to see what we are doing about what is theirs?
Some of those who spoke before me asked whether the Indians were consulted. That is one of the questions I wanted to ask. I hope the minister will answer that question. I am not sure whether the Indians were consulted in the preparation of this brief and confusing bill, because it seems to display- this has been mentioned by others, also, notably by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) - a form of paternalism which has marked the attitude of governments toward the native people. I submit, for the consideration of the House and the minister in particular,
October 21, 1974

that this paternalism underlaid the events on the opening day of this parliament.
The new minister had evidence at the opening of this session that there was unrest. There is, obviously, unrest. Those manifestations were not made apparent simply for the joy of it. The minister has evidence that there is something seriously wrong. I hope we are embarking upon a new era of relations with the Indian people, approaching them in a different way, consulting them and having them take part in the administration of their own affairs. There are several bands in my riding. They are managed by able, competent administrators, people who enjoy the confidence of the membership of the bands. These are the people who must be consulted.
I should like to comment on one or two of the clauses of the bill. I notice that in clause 2 mention is made of Indian lands. Indian lands, we read, include lands which have been surrendered in accordance with the Indian Act". This led me right back to the Indian Act to find out just how it is that land can be surrendered, and under what terms. What is this about Indians surrendering their land? It is part of the paternalism we should, surely, be getting away from. Surrender is obviously only exercisable under the terms in which the Indian land originally came into the hands of the provinces, so we are left with the acts of accession of the provinces to confederation. Surrender could be in absolute or in qualified terms and involves some or all the rights attached to these lands-surface rights, subsoil rights, water rights, the right of passage, and so on. Are we sure these are the same in all the acts of accession of the provinces? I am not sure. These are questions which ought to be raised in committee.
The hon. member for Greenwood pointed out that the only reference to bands has to do with the case in which there is to be a reduction in royalties. I find this most peculiar. I wonder why there was no provision in the original regulations for determination of what the royalties should be-an increase or a reduction, whatever might be determined. We should look into this question a good deal more carefully. There must, of course, be provision for consultation with the bands. As to the word "surrender", once again let me suggest this is a word we must try to avoid.
I wish the new minister well. He is faced with a new movement among the Indian people, one which is likely to be extremely difficult to deal with. I want to assure him he can count on the co-operation of the party to which I belong, provided he takes the Indians into his confidence.
My hon. friend from Peace River has mentioned the uncertainty surrounding the validity of the original regulations, those of 1966. Clause 3 begins with the words "For greater certainty," and so on, and immediately refers to a number of subsections and section 45 of the Indian oil and gas regulations "expressed to have been made pursuant to paragraph 57(c) of the Indian Act." Well, 57(c) provides that certain regulations can be made. Why must this be repeated in the bill before us? Are these not valid regulations? I certainly hope they are, and I gather from the look on the minister's face that he hopes so, too. Because if they are not, we may be in serious trouble.
Indian Affairs
Later on in clause 3 we read that these subsections, and so on-
-shall for all purposes have and continue to have, until revoked by the governor in council, the same force and effect as if they had been made on that day-
In other words, on March 28, 1974, Mr. Speaker, I found that this order in council is simply an amendment to the original one. It says that subject to these regulations, the royalty on oil and gas shall be collected in such manner as may be prescribed by the minister. Here, again, we find the great patron of the Indian people. He is acting on their behalf, with or without consultation. I find this wording to be most unfortunate.
Just for fun, I compared the new regulations with the old regulations. I found that the provisions of clause 4 of the bill before us repeat some, but only some, of the articles of the original order in council. Why only some? Why does the bill not repeat the whole of those provisions so that parliament may know what they are, so that we, together with those who, hopefully, will benefit from the royalties may know exactly what needs to be done in order that the royalties may be collected. If hon. members read through paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) they will find a repetition of much of the original order in council which is published in volume 100 of part II of the Canada Gazette of July 27, 1966. I might just as well put that on record in Hansard because I believe it is relevant to the proper consideration of the bill before us.
In short, it seems to me this is an untidy piece of legislation. I do not doubt the minister's good intentions; I have confidence that he intends to go about dealing with the problems of our Indian people in the proper way. Nevertheless, I think he should have tidied up this legislation before presenting it to the House. In any case, the proposals certainly deserve to be given close examination in committee. I can assure the minister of the constructive comments and co-operation of members on this side of the House in consideration of this particular measure.
One comment which the minister made seems worth mentioning in my closing remarks. If I heard him correctly, he said something about Indian bands which had got to the situation where they could not make the rapid adjustments required over the last year in terms of the energy resources of this country. Why cannot they adjust rapidly, Madam Speaker? The rest of the world has had to adjust quickly. I suggest it is because of the paternalism of government. I think the government has inherited that paternalism; I do not blame the minister for it. I suggest they should be able to respond quickly, and through the consultative process they can be made to respond quickly to changing circumstances.
Like others who have spoken before me, I regret that this legislation, though in a better form and not in this untidy way, was not brought forward when the regulations were amended earlier this year. Then we would have been able to examine the complete bag of tricks. For example, I find clause 7 a little disturbing because of what I said about clause 5. We are expected to confer upon the government, which in all honesty has not shown the greatest devotion to the cause of letting the Indians help them-
October 21, 1974

Indian Affairs
selves-or for that matter, other people in this country, too-authority to fix by proclamation the coming into effect of a very important clause in this bill.
Therefore, the bill should go quickly to committee, where we undertake to give it honest and constructive criticism. But we want the Indian people to have a voice in this matter, and this may mean amending the Indian Act. If that is the case, let us do it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
I am happy to have the opportunity of saying a few words on this bill to permit the drafting of new rules and regulations relating to the oil and gas industry and the native people. For too long the government has caused uncertainty because it has failed to set out in a positive and concrete manner a policy respecting oil and gas and the interests not only of our first Canadians, the Indian people, but indeed all Canadians.
It gives me some pride to speak today about our first Canadians. When I entered the House I was the member for the constituency of Bow River, which at that time comprised part city and part country. In the area around Calgary were situated two reservations, namely, Morley to the west of Calgary, and the Blackfoot reservation to the southeast of Calgary. Both those areas were within the boundary of the Bow River constituency. Today, the Blackfoot reservation is in the constituency of Crowfoot, which is named after one of the famous chiefs of the Blackfoot reservation. Morley is, I believe, in the constituency of Rocky Mountain. This change resulted from redistribution. Palliser still remains pretty well in the former Bow River area, with the exception of the two reservations and the surrounding farming community.
Since I have been in the House of Commons, as well as all my life as a citizen of western Canada, I have had much to do with the early Canadians. I feel there is no more important task today than studying this legislation, which will give the cabinet power to make rules and regulations governing some of the resources on Indian lands which are not only within the jurisdiction of the provinces but, far more extensively, within the jurisdiction of the federal government. This legislation is extremely important to the economic and social welfare of our early Canadians. I do know what kind of language to use in describing their treatment, but they have been treated so shabbily in the past that we as Canadians should never boast about what we have done for our native people. If ever we have discriminated against a class of people, particularly since confederation, it is our early Canadians, and in many ways this discrimination is continuing.
Rules and regulations of this kind, which the government sometimes change overnight and change the name of the game, are important economically to these people, as I say. One has only to visit the two reservations I have mentioned to realize this fact. I hope I am not thought to be egotistical, but I am an honorary chief of both the

Morley and the Blackfoot reservations. I was made an honorary chief of the Morley reservation just before I entered the House of Commons because I fought a trial on their behalf which was successful for their betterment. After I became a member of parliament I was named Big Beaver, a chief of the Blackfoot reservation. I know that this honour is also shared by another English-speaking Canadian who reached the height of being prime minister of this country, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). In both those bands he is an honorary chief. The Hon. Ellen Fairclough, who was minister of Indian affairs in the Diefenbaker government, was not only made a princess of the Blackfoot reservation but was also-you will appreciate this, Madam Speaker-made a chief of the Blackfoot tribe. I was at that very colourful ceremony. So it is with deep interest and feeling that I speak on this matter today.
Pages of rules and regulations are all very well, but the most important thing we should consider today is the creation of a national oil policy for this country so as to encourage development and exploration of petroleum and natural gas reserves to guarantee that Canada will always be self-sufficient in their supply. Unfortunately, under the present administration which was re-elected again in July, the policies we have had have done everything to discourage the development of petroleum and natural gas resources. Since these policies have discouraged exploration and development of these resources in parts of the country under provincial jurisdiction, then they will discourage them on Indian reservations and in the Arctic, on lands under the federal jurisdiction and control of our native people. That is why the first thing to consider is the development of a policy to encourage exploration.
There seems to be a feeling right across the country that it is a great sin to receive a reasonable return from development and exploration. I ask hon. members to remember that the oil industry is not like the competition that exists between little storekeepers. It is a very tough and competitive international industry thoughout the world. Unless tax and other incentives are provided for the industry, the industry will take its capital and drilling equipment and move elsewhere.
When I was at home last Friday I read in the Calgary Herald a headline and an article in relation to this whole situation. Calgary is a flourishing city which has contributed greatly to the economic welfare of this nation. It has done much to provide incentives and motivation in respect of exploration for oil and gas throughout Alberta. As a result of these incentives and encouragements Alberta has become the producer of 86 per cent of crude petroleum and natural gas in western Canada. The headline to which I referred is not surprising, as a similar article appeared in the Financial Post last year. The article reads that drilling rigs are now leaving Alberta in drowes and going to the United States. I suggest that in fact they are going to the United States, to Mexico and to areas in the North Sea because the economic climate is much better for the industry.
Let me emphasize that rules, regulations and legislation will not solve the basic problem in respect of incentives. In an article which appeared in the Financial Post over a year
October 21, 1974

ago, dealing with development in this industry as a result of the gouging of the oil and gas industries by the federal government without consultation with the provinces, we find reference to the implementation of a system of taxation totally inequitable and unfair to the industry. We suggested the same thing during the election campaign. I will not read the whole article, because of its length; but on June 15, 1974, during the election campaign my leader made a speech in which he made it clear that it is not equitable to have the royalties charged by the province or the federal government not treated as an expense subtracted from the taxable income upon which the federal tax is based.
When we analyse the tax structures of this nation, we read the economic reports. They indicate that no nation today takes a bigger slice of the taxation pie, particularly in respect of resource industries. Can you imagine the reaction of the manufacturing industry in Ontario or Quebec to a tax on the textile industry and a super tax charge on the first tax? It is tax charges on tax dollars. I suggest that everyone would scream, just as the people of Alberta are screaming about this tax which is totally inequitable and unfair. The minister knows about this situation, as he was raised in Edmonton. I knew his father. He comes from a very distinguished family. He knows as well as I do that to put a tax on the price and whatever profit is left, plus royalties, represents a federal tax on a tax. This practice is totally unjust and inequitable.
We have heard a great deal about foreign capital. About 96 per cent of the drilling industry in Canada is owned by Canadians, not Americans, Japanese or the British. Yet Canadian equipment, administration and know-how are moving elsewhere. I have never believed the stuff peddled by my hon. friends in the NDP to the effect that no more oil will be found in Canada. I suppose that in 1941 they did not think oil would found in Alberta. Let me suggest that only by developing and exploring do you find these resources. They still exist only if found. We still have the tar sands and we have found other oil fields on the prairies. We are still finding fields in the Arctic. These fields cannot be found if the companies pick up their tools and go elsewhere-and that is what they are doing because of unfair taxation.
The Financial Post warned the Liberal government a year ago about its being more interested in getting votes than in seeing development take place. Let me read one paragraph from this article, as follows:
Klimchuk's company has just raised $3 million-$4 million in equity money in Canada and now is in the process of adding another $5 million in drilling-fund money raised in the U S.
"Under existing conditions we are planning to invest more than 90 per cent of that money ... in the U.S."
The United States provides depletion allowances and incentives. That administration would never think of placing taxes upon taxes and royalties. The article continues:
Almost all western oilmen prefer Washington's proposed method of taxing the industry ... to the current Canadian system.
The same article reads:
Hudson's Bay Oil & Gas Co., one of western Canada's most active oil and gas exploration firms, has just established a foreign exploration headquarters in Houston. The company's entire international exploration program, including a stepped-up U.S. operation, will be operated out of that centre.
Indian Affairs
We have heard a lot about the Home Oil Company in the last few years. Let me read this reference in the article:
Home Oil Co., one of the largest Canadian independents, is presently looking for an exploration headquarters in Houston.
"Recent events have certainly improved the relative attractiveness of U.S. exploration," Home president R. F. Phillips told FP.
"There is no doubt that Canadian activity is going to increase there very considerably during the next few years."
I suggest that is because we have this present tax structure. The minister should get together with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and examine this whole matter of royalties in order that they may be written off as an expense against taxable income. Surely that is only equitable and just; and this is required if we are to save the day. The headline in the Calgary Herald points out that drilling companies are leaving Alberta and going elsewhere. There are still many areas in Canada which can be termed have-not areas. It is not so long ago that Alberta could not pay the interest on its bonds. Time passes quickly, and as a result of development in the petroleum and natural gas industries, and by increasing agricultural know-how, Alberta has become one of the three or four "have" provinces. This was not done by gouging the industry; it was done by providing incentive and motivation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext: Speak about the bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
I am speaking about the bill. Obviously, the hon. member does not know what this is all about. He would like to have a pretty book of regulations. But what is the point of regulations in respect of petroleum and gas if the drilling companies quit their activities? If the hon. member can learn that, it might be helpful. That hon. member has always spoken with the same degree of mentality he has exercised today.
When talking about the subject matter of this bill, we are talking about jobs. If we encourage exploration and development on Indian reservations or in areas under the jurisdiction of our native people, we will be providing jobs. I ask hon. members what this would do for the housing and social problems of these people. They would find themselves with royalties that would swell their band funds.
We must examine the conditions under which our Indians now live. The problem was referred to at the opening of this parliament. Everything else we might do will be child's play if we do not do something for the Indian people of Canada. To begin with, let us give them the right to decide that people with know-how can drill on their lands. In this way they will obtain royalties with which they can get into housing and other areas and increase their standard of living. That is the important point I am trying to make.
The minister is travelling across this country talking with various premiers. Unless he can reach some agreement in respect of rules and regulations, what we are doing here is merely window-dressing. Parliament can legislate and look busy, but if it legislates in respect of something that is superfluous, then it means nothing and we are wasting our time. Let us consider what has gone on. In 1969, the federal government enacted tax legislation to increase the effective tax rates of the petroleum indus-

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
try. This legislation terminates, in 1976, automatic depletion allowances on production revenue.
In 1970, the federal government suspended portions of its land regulations, thus creating serious uncertainty for industry in these important exploration theatres. In 1973, the federal government imposed a crude oil price freeze and an export tax on crude oil exports. Let us consider that for a few moments. During the election campaign we heard a good deal about price controls. Most of our opponents forgot about that and wanted to talk about wage control. The whole incomes policy of the Conservative Party was criticized. Of course, that is what the election was about. The situation is that it seems to be wrong to establish prices on any commodity, although in western Canada it seems to be the practice of the Liberal government to set prices on wheat, oil and, at one time, on cattle. On April 23, 1974, long before the "funeral" took place, the minister dealt with this matter in the committee. He said that certainly they would have to take into consideration lumber and potash and, I suppose, other resources. They might have taken a look at them, but the only people who have had their prices set are those in the resource industries.
I know what industry means to the industrial might of this nation. It had to come to grips with a very difficult problem. Let us consider lumber. Lumber was priced high because of exports to Japan. There has been a falling off now in lumber prices, but nothing has been done about that, or about potash. It has been done just in respect of the industries on the prairies. This is what is called discrimination.
During the election campaign I moved around a good deal and had an opportunity to talk to people. I never found anyone in any part of Canada who would not agree that what is equitable for one part of this country should be equitable for all parts of the country. Surely, on the question of taxation alone, the government should give ground. The federal government on May 6, 1974, proposed in its budget new tax provisions for the oil industry. These contained the new feature of including in taxable income, royalties, surcharges, mineral taxes, and so on, payable to the provincial governments.
This feature alone would seriously impair the petroleum industry's future investment capability. Not only would it drive Canadian capital out of the country, but it would discourage any other capital to come in, because this is a very highly competitive industry. For every well which has proved successful in Alberta, I am told by top geologists that nine are found to be dry holes. Today, with inflation, the cost of drilling a well has increased five or six times. It is a very expensive operation.
If we can encourage development on Indian lands where Indians can enjoy the benefits, let us do so; but let us have some tax incentives in this country so that development can take place and so we wrill not kill the industry. It will not be long before we will have no crude petroleum or natural gas because of the policies of this government. If the Indians are to receive anything from the petroleum or natural gas, there must be pipelines. We have had the yo-yo program of the Liberal government for ten years. I

have heard this and other Liberal prime ministers say they intended to build the pipeline to Montreal. It is not built. If there is encouragement, we have the potential to build the pipeline in Canada. It should be built so that there will be the necessary transportation facility for these products, to encourage production and so there will be a market in Canada for Canadian production of oil and gas.
The great railway development brought the country together. Surely we have here another vision. The development of the pipeline would guarantee Quebec and the maritimes that they would always have sufficient supply of natural gas and crude petroleum and by-products, such as gasoline for automobiles, at a price which is equitable and similar to the price people pay for these products where they are found and brought out of the ground. We must give the Canadian people a chance. We must give the Indian people, who are the first Canadians, a chance so that their social and economic life and, indeed, their moral spirit is lifted; so that a new day will dawn in Canada for people who have been discriminated against for more than 100 years.
