subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON FOOD AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take the lead in establishing a World Commission on Food and Resources, under the auspices of the United Nations, to compile a comprehensive and regular inventory of the existing world foodstuffs and resources essential for substenance; each nation shall be required to report annually (with quarterly amendments) on the state of its own self-sufficiency and on its ability to transfer key foodstuffs and resources to more needy nations; the Commission shall have the authority to transfer designated food and resources from member nations equal in amount to their expenditures on defence.
He said: Madam Speaker, this opportunity for hon. members during private members' hours is one of the most important rights and privileges extended to all members of parliament with regard to subjects which members feel are important in the conduct of public business. In the years during which I have had an opportunity to speak in parliament on a variety of subjects, I do not think any subject has presented itself as being of such major importance as the one chosen for my motion this afternoon.
At the outset may I say that I do not wish members opposite, or people anywhere, to think the motion I have presented is in itself the be-all and end-all of the problem to which it is addressed. I refer, of course, to the impending world food crisis which increasingly has become a matter of public concern, not only in those countries which are directly experiencing famine but also in countries of overwhelming affluence such as our own. We are increasingly realizing that this is one world. While some may live in affluence, many more may live in the degradation of poverty. It is no longer possible for us to ignore this fact. Eventually it will have an overwhelming impact upon us.
I am delighted that this motion was placed high on the list for debate, because all members will have a chance to discuss it now in the context of the world food conference which is to take place in Rome on November 5. While the motion is not directed solely to that particular conference, it is certainly the essence of the conference itself. This is the first time that the nations of the world, at the ministerial level, have agreed to meet and discuss the dimensions of the growing food crisis in this decade and to try to see what medium and long term solutions can be discovered. In the first instance, the proposal for the conference grew out of a meeting of non-aligned nations a little over a year ago and was encouraged by a speech delivered to the United Nations on September 24, 1973, by Dr. Henry Kissinger, who said:
The growing threat to the world's food supply deserves the urgent attention of this assembly. Since 1969 global consumption of cereals has risen more rapidly than production-
He could have said "since 1972". The growing discrepancy between the ability to produce food on a global scale, crop failures and recurring drought conditions have created an alarming condition. He went on to say:
Food and Resources
Stocks are at the lowest levels in years.
That is even more true in the fall of 1974. To continue:
We now face the prospect that-even with bumper crops-the world may not rebuild its seriously depleted reserves in this decade.
No one country can cope with this problem. The United States therefore proposes:
That a world food conference be organized under United Nations auspices in 1974 to discuss ways to maintain adequate food supplies and to harness the efforts of all nations to meet the hunger and malnutrition resulting from natural disasters.
That nations in a position to do so offer technical assistance in the conservation of food.
What we are faced with, Madam Speaker, is not just the continual question of occasional famines or shortages of food in one place or the other. We are faced with the most basic problem of all, which is not-as some people suggested recently-that there are too many people in the world, although population growth is a factor. It is not that there is any fundamental reason why the world cannot produce more food, although production increases will require unusual, innovative and bold schemes in order to be successful; and we cannot even say that there is an insufficiency of food aid, because aid alone will never be enough and food is wasted daily on a large scale, even in our own country. We can say there is maldistribution of much of the world's food supply at the present time. We must admit this is the case when we learn that the protein consumption of the average North American is five times that of the average citizen of India. We know, because figures have been quoted from time to time, that in North America we feed more to our cattle than the total cereal consumption of the populations of both India and China. We know, too, that we feed more to our pets than is fed to the populations of many countries.
In an article in yesterday's New York Times, headed "32 Nations Close to Starvation," Boyce Rensberger wrote:
In the judgment of United Nations experts, 32 countries in the world are so poor and so short of food that crop failures and the high prices of grain, fertilizer and petroleum threaten them with bankruptcy and their people with starvation.
Madam Speaker, I have not time to list the various countries and the average daily caloric intake which would indicate the low level of sustenance of hundreds of thousands of our fellow citizens on this planet. I would urge hon. members who can find the time, however, to read the article. The sources that I could quote to support the accusation of maldistribution of food resources are almost unlimited. Mr. Maurice Strong, a Canadian who is director-general of the United Nations Environmental Organization, spoke to the Ottawa Canadian Club in February of this year and said:
In one decade, 1959-68, the United Nations alone used more resources than all of the world's peoples in all of previous history.
I am concerned not only because the situation is bad, but because it is growing worse. It is growing worse because there are suggestions that the advantage that Canada now has, as a major food producer and exporter, can be turned to some kind of political advantage. Some hon. members may have seen an article in the Globe and Mail on September 23 written by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) regarding President Ford's recent speech to the United Nations. The hon. member wrote:

October 21, 1974
Food and Resources
The president's implied threat to withhold food from the Arab world as a lever in getting a reasonable Arab policy toward Israel and reasonable world oil prices could mean a totally new and powerful status for Canada in international affairs.
Later in the article he wrote:
It seems clear that Canada must agree with the goals defined by President Ford at the United Nations.
An hon. member suggests that agri-power is indeed the temptation that was laid before Canada and was clearly stated by the President of the United States. It is this kind of disturbing opinion that must alert us to the realization that if we are to deal reasonably, intelligently, humanely and with justice with this major problem, it will not be because we take a narrow view of the good fortune that Canada has known to date. I am concerned that we not enter into some kind of food politics game with the lives of men, women and children. It would seem to me that, in the first instance, we must be aware that some of the objectives we have been pursuing as a nation and as individuals will no longer be acceptable. Some of the ideals and hopes we have for the future of life on this planet will have to be tempered by the realities which are becoming increasingly clear to us.
I was extremely pleased and surprised, following the tabling of this motion, to read a report of a speech by Bishop Power of Antigonish to the fourth synod of bishops presently meeting at the Vatican. Speaking of the need for Canadians to take a new look at their own situation and responsibility in the world community, and urging Canadians to respond to that situation, Bishop Power said:
-we asked our fellow Canadians to question the goals of our wasteful economic system, to modify their affluent eating habits, to substitute other foods for meat, to give more generously to neighbours in need, to develop new educational programs leading to changed lifestyles.
Then he said:
But sharing by the private sector is not enough. We are asking our country, through its policy makers, to contribute to a world food bank.
I have not discussed this with Bishop Power. While the world food bank the bishop proposes may be different from a world commission on food and resources which I propose in this motion, its aims are the same. We both realize that we cannot depend on the capricious whims of nations and individuals if we are to resolve the growing food crisis. Interestingly enough, the bishop dealt not only with what is in the first part of my motion, but also with the relationship between defence spending and what we must spend on other areas if society is to survive. He said: Disarmament should be accompanied by substantial transformation of the economic and political structures which generate these profound injustices. We should insist that the money wasted to keep peoples in chains be used to procure freedom and daily bread for all men.
At one time we heard the slogan, much in vogue, "Choose either guns or butter." I suspect that the peoples of the world must now choose between bread and bombs. If we are not prepared to make that decision, it will be made for us. Norman E. Borlaug, 1970 winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, said recently:
International granaries of food reserves, financed by all nations, should be established for use in case of need ... Man can and must prevent the tragedy of famine in the future instead of trying, with pious regret, to salvage the human wreckage of the famine, as he has so

often done in the past. Plans for international grain reserves have been put forward eight times since 1946, and each time they have floundered on questions of national sovereignty.
A plan on this subject is to be put forward at the world food conference. Its effectiveness will depend on what the government of the United States thinks, as the United States is the key to an agreement on world grain reserves. Dr. Marei, secretary-general of the Rome conference in November, has already proposed as an agenda item the creation of a world food authority with supranational powers. Only if we pay attention to the vision of such men can we avoid the prospect of a holocaust in the history of this planet. That is why, at a meeting in which the Canadian Council for International Co-operation participated in Ottawa, following a meeting of mor e than 70 non-governmental agencies concerned with the world food crisis and the world food conference, it was said:
Canada should support the creation of a world food authority, and that the voting power of the world food authority be on the basis of equal voting representation between donor and recipient nations in line with the UN declaration on the establishment of a new economic order.
We must remember this. Frankly, I am disappointed that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and senior government officials have said so little about Canada's position at the conference which is to take place in just over two weeks. It is, therefore, important for members on all sides of the House to express themselves forcibly on the aims of the conference which, I submit, is bound up with the substance of the motion I have put forward.
What will be the most effective way to help? What will be the most acceptable instrument? Obviously, the government will not be influenced by members of the House alone; it will be influenced by public opinion. Frankly, I think the government will face difficulty in moving forward in this area owing to lack of informed and public discussion in this country on the topic with which we are concerned.
We can no longer follow our suicidal priorities which put armaments ahead of food. In this connection I wish to quote the words of Robert McNamara, former secretary of defence of the United States, who said:
Surely one of the most foolish follies of man all through history is his almost incurable insistence on spending more energy and wealth in waging war than in preventing it.
Mr. McNamara is now president of the World Bank and a leading figure in seeking solutions to the world food crisis. Members on all sides of the House who are concerned about the problem will realize that we need imaginative solutions. By itself, the problem will not go away but will become incalculably worse. When I was preparing my speech this afternoon I looked at some figures and learned that approximately 14,000 people are starving to death each day-two-thirds of them children. Further research has revealed the figure to be in the order of 40,000 a day. Actually, we do not know how many are starving to death, how many succumb to the most unacceptable disease brought on by lack of the staff of life.
I invite all hon. members to support this motion, and I urge the government in the strongest terms to allow full discussion of this question in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
October 21, 1974

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON FOOD AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) dealt with a most relevant issue in presenting a motion on the problem of food in the world.
The motion contains many points such as a request that the countries report on their level of autonomy. Experience teaches that some countries, mainly developing ones, cannot or do not want to make such reports. The transfer of food and resources is already regulated by international arrangements like those existing now such as the World Food Program. Canada has a tradition of opposing the creation of new international institutions, particularly when such institutions exist and seem to be able to do the work. The FAO is now studying a project on world food security. One important aspect of this document concerns the establishment of an information system on food, the main goals of which are to collect, analyse and disseminate information on the grain overall situation and forecasts. At the present time, Canada is providing the FAO with information concerning our production and stocks. We have indicated our intention to continue to provide this information through the world food information system.
A World Conference on Food will be held this coming November in Rome. A number of suggestions made by the hon. member will be examined on this occasion. Canada is one of the main producers taking part in the World Food Program. The Canadian contribution to this program since 1963 amounts to $131 million. Canada is the biggest supplier taking part in the World Food Program. For many years, Canada has held enormous stocks of grains.
One cannot ignore the impact of this motion on prices and trade. Farmers alone cannot be expected to help poor countries; our society as a whole must participate in this endeavour.
Perhaps it might be more useful to support measures aiming at increasing production within developing countries, thereby reducing their dependency on food aid.
Mr. Speaker, one needs but note the number of times the matter was brought up in this House, the attention it was given by the media, and the preparations launched into by international organizations, governments and private concerns for the coming World Food Conference, to become aware of its importance. The hustle and bustle reflects the increasing concern of the international community in this regard. Many are those who wonder how the rapidly increasing world population will manage to feed itself.
Reflecting on the matter of world food reserves, the hon. member for Egmont draws our attention to one of the main aspects of the current discussion on food problems. Like my colleague, Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be desirable to improve the world food situation information system. I would like to add to this, however: that system is a fundamental element of a much greater problem, that of "world food security" which consists mainly in keeping world food reserves at an adequate level. Improving the information system is closely related to the need for an efficient cereal reserves system, as well as to those in the
Food and Resources
fields of production, consumption, price setting and international trade in basic agricultural products.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) spoke of this complex network of problems, of the difficulties in finding easy solutions, in his address to the FAO conference almost a year ago. He said, and I quote:
"The world Food Security Proposal made by the Director-General is the result of the short world food supply. It is designed to lead to relative stability in the cumulative production, pricing and stocks of food around the world. These levels are intended to vary with need as estimated by consultation among nations. The proposal suggests food stocks could be much better dispersed in all countries rather than be held by a few major producers. The Director-General also stresses the voluntary nature of participation and the need for better information.
Canada has already gone on record urging every nation, not just those who are traditional surplus food producers, to support and cooperate with FAO in this task. Importers as well as exporters have both a concern and a responsibility. The question of adequate grain inventories is of major concern to Canada. We have, for a number of years, carried at our expense approximately 40 per cent of the total world wheat reserve. We are prepared to move in the direction of a food security scheme, but we have found from past experience that some nations are reluctant to share costs for maintaining reserves, let alone the costs of having too large reserves looked upon as surpluses overhanging international markets and pricing farmers out of needed regular increased production.
A storage program is desirable, indeed it is a necessary feature of trying to maintain a world food supply."
The proposal-that is the proposed world food security action plan-made by FAO Secretary General Boerma, to which my colleague referred, deals with all the aspects of the problem of world food security. In substance, it proposes that the governments of member states pledge cooperation to ensure at all times an adequate supply of basic foods, particularly grain, to avoid serious food shortages in case of bad generalized crops or natural catastrophes, to allow a continued increase in production and reduced variations in both production and prices.
Furthermore, member states recognizing that food security should be ensured in many ways, especially by reinforcing the farming capacity of developing countries, by appropriate national stocking policies, food help programs and other action, including long term trade agreements. They promise to take national and international action to encourage fast growth of food production as required, and to give special help to developing countries, which are very exposed to crop variations and face increasing consumer demand.
On the other hand, as concerns the stocking policy, it is recommended that all governments, in accordance with their institutional and constitutional requirements first, implement a grain stocking policy which takes into account those of other countries and ensures minimal reserves of major grains at the world level, second, review or establish stocking objectives, or take action in this area, to maintain their grain reserves or those of groups of

October 21, 1974
Food and Resources
countries, at least at the levels judged necessary, so that an uninterrupted supply will be ensured, including in emergency situations brought about by bad crops or natural disasters, third, take the necessary action for the stocks to be replenished as soon as possible following shortages, when they have fallen below established minimums.
Finally, the suggestion specifies that in the case of serious food shortages, the member states that have larger reserves than they need to meet national needs and emergency supplies will make a commitment to authorize exports at reasonable conditions.
These various approaches to the problem of world food security are striking in that they recognize the complexity of this problem, Mr. Speaker. There are no simple answers to this problem. On this point, I do not agree with the hon. member for Egmont. He suggests that a new organization could resolve at all the problems together by maintaining a satisfactory level of food supplies and by ensuring the transfer of these supplies to the most needy areas.
But how would these transfers be made? What effect would they have on international trade agreements or on present methods of food assistance distribution? How could we assure the Canadian farmer that he will continue to receive an appropriate price for his products? And who would pay for these products?
The Minister of Agriculture knew about these complications when he said, and I quote:
-farmers must be enticed and encouraged to steadily greater production by the assurance that they make a reasonable living. Canada has the most efficient farmers in the world. Their efficiency has increased far more rapidly than that of our industrial sector. Yet even they need a paying reward and security of income if they are expected to increase production for world-wide use.
And Mr. Whelan, concerning the effect that surpluses might have on world markets, added:
Canada can also support the need for assistance to developing countries to facilitate the desired adjustments. But Canada also supports the need for action and policies to deal with world surplus conditions that ruin the structure and investment, the very basis of a guaranteed growing supply of food around the world. Nowhere in the world can producers be expected to risk either investment or a lifetime's labor to have it cut from under them by short time surpluses. The result is a stagnation of production potential.
The report of the third session of the preparatory committee of the World Food Conference suggested something along the the sames line:
Most delegates have agreed that if trade is to fill its role it must maintain free and ordered movements at stable prices and ensure, at reasonable prices, a market for exporters and a supply for importers.
The committee also remarked:
-that it is essential that the main producing and consuming countries adhere to the suggested plan of action so to fully attain the objectives of world food security.
The committee also acknowledged the need to solve certain practical and technical problems so that the action planned might be efficient and it expressed the hope that those solutions might be elaborated by the appropriate intergovernmental agencies of the FAO.
It was agreed that, given the present shortage, food reserves must be made up gradually so as not to disturb the market. The creation of food reserves will be insured only if a suitable balance between supply and demand has

already been achieved. The necessity of providing financial and technical assistance to developing countries to help them create and maintain food reserves was also pointed out.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a last remark before concluding. Suitable trade agreements, distribution of food assistance, a system of reserves, stocks, all that is not enough to ensure world food security. We must also give much greater attention to the agricultural development of the countries that are in the greatest need of food stocks to feed their huge population. Besides, it was mentioned in the Boerma proposal that the essential interest shown in this endeavour by the developing countries, in order to achieve the objectives of a world food security, requires guarantees as to sufficient grain stocks and accordingly an accelerated growth rate of their agricultural production. Such an increase requires on the part of developing countries a continual review of their agricultural program and of the various alternatives available to them, and implies as well the active support of the international community to the development programs of those countries within the national development program of each.
The international organizations concerned, working in financial and technical sectors, the developed countries and other possible donor countries should most urgently take the necessary steps to enable developing countries to get financial, technical and material aid, particularly fertilizers and other elements that are essential to the increase of their agricultural production. The proposal goes on in these terms: The international community must make an important contribution, through low rate food and financial assistance, or through subsidies, in order to maintain grain supplies in developing countries, particularly emergency supplies, at their proper level, to determine what supply facilities are best according to local situations, and to provide advice on storage problems and related policies within national development programs. Developed countries and other possible donors, as well as the international and regional development organizations concerned, should contribute complementary help to the identification and pooling of resources required to meet those objectives.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should consider several solutions. There has been to date considerable studies indeed in preparation for the FAO conference to be held in Rome. Should grain producing countries store sufficient amounts of grain for future needs, or should every country be required to provide for its own needs and store at least enough food for a year's consumption?
Mr. Speaker, it was my honour and pleasure to attend FAO meetings in Rome last October, and I was amazed by the amount of technological help developed countries could contribute. I heard speeches by representatives of some countries on the question of food. They even said the stage of "harnessed" agriculture had not yet been reached. We can therefore imagine how underdeveloped countries, which have not yet reached that stage of "harnessed" agriculture, may grow their own food.
Mr. Speaker, we should put the emphasis on the possibility of helping the developing countries in technical terms to improve their situation in that area and become eventually self-sufficient in respect of food.
October 21, 1974

Mr. Speaker, after all those thoughts, I find that a lot more aspects must be taken into consideration before we could be prepared to set up a concrete world food program.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON FOOD AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend very warmly the initiative of the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) in introducing this subject. It is one of profound importance. The crisis is a very real one and Canada's opportunity to make an important contribution lies before us, particularly in connection with the World Conference on Food in Rome which the hon. member mentioned.
I agree with him there is a sort of insanity attached to our choice of priorities. When I was at the conference in the Chateau Laurier the other day we were told by a knowledgeable gentleman, I think it was Mr. Jackson of the FAO, that a substantial program for increasing food supplies in the developing countries could be put under way for roughly $5 billion. Although $5 billion sounds like quite a lot of money, the world today is spending over $200 billion a year on armaments. I suggest that a world that cannot look after its basic food needs but devotes enormous sums to armaments is a world in which priorities have gone very far astray.
In bringing this matter forward I think the hon. member has done us a great service. I do not propose to discuss the details of his motion. I am not sure that the word commission pleases me very much, because it seems to imply more inquiries. I suspect that what is needed is not so much a commission of inquiry; FAO, for one organization, is extremely well informed of the facts. What we will need will be more action.
The other day Dr. Waldheim, Secretary General of the United Nations, in answer to a declaration by a number of scientists that was brought to his attention, said that basic food was the one essential, undebatable core of a life of dignity and decency. He also added that all aspirations for peace, growth, creativity and social justice, of individuals as well as of nations, would have a hollow ring unless we grappled with the problem of meeting basic food needs.
This is not really a new problem. There has been malnutrition in the world for some years. One can throw around figures like 460 million people suffering chronic hunger and malnutrition. But, apart from this, the recent drop in food reserves brings into the realm of likelihood, if not probability, vast loss of life through outright famine in different parts of the world unless adequate steps are taken to prevent it.
I will not go into all the things that should be done; this may be the job of the conference. The hon. member for Egmont mentioned setting up a world food bank, and it seems to me that this is an essential part of the machinery. The hon. member referred to a world food authority. I do not think it matters whether you call it a bank or an authority, but it should be internationally managed and given the means to do the job. I think that is one of the first prerequisites.
Another is to recognize that the greatest contribution to alleviating the food crisis throughout the world is to
Food and Resources
enable developing countries to expand their food production. In the developed countries like Canada perhaps there are some things that can be done and should be done, and whatever we do should take into account the interests and rights of the farmers who are the producers of food. But it is in the developing countries that there is the greatest opportunity to increase food production through technological changes, changes that we have already made and which could be made available to these other countries. Of course, what is useful under Canadian conditions may not be very useful in India or Bangladesh, and research will have to be adapted to different countries in which it is sought to increase food production.
Research should be vastly expanded. We need a crash program to increase the supply of pesticides and fertilizers. One of the reasons for the present food crisis is that the price of energy has put fertilizers and pesticides beyond the reach of many farmers and producers in developing countries.
Food aid is not enough. It is helpful and may be absolutely necessary, but in itself it is not enough. If food aid is to be viable it must complement our trade policies and enable developing countries independently to achieve economic growth within their own borders.
In an extremely eloquent address to the Canadian Jewish Congress on June 25 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said something that I think is very appropriate to this debate. He said that he hoped that Canada's presence in the world would be judged by its humanism and pursuit of social justice. He said Canada's foreign policy would be meaningless if this were not carried out, as it would not reflect the character of Canadians. He then referred to the Elizabethan poet John Donne, who said that "every man's death diminishes me". The Prime Minister added that this quotation should guide our foreign policy as it guides our domestic policy. Compassion, the Prime Minister stated, must have no geographic focus, nor must our geographic efforts have geographic limitations. With these words I believe all members of the House can agree.
We must put this into practice and use what influence we have, not, as the hon. member for Egmont said, with the desire to gain political advantage for ourselves, but to help out, in a spirit of brotherhood, the cause of humanity.
I think I have indicated as clearly as I can our deep concern about the subject raised by the hon. member. I hope that the government of Canada will take the matter extremely seriously. We are pleased to hear that the minister was thinking of going to Rome as our head delegate. I hope he will take some members of parliament with him, perhaps from different parties, as well as some non-governmental representatives. I say so because I do not think this is a matter just for the experts and bureaucrats; this is a matter in which the generosity and goodwill of the Canadian people should be challenged, and I believe they will be challenged. I know many Canadians who already are deeply concerned and who will be watching what we do at the conference with the greatest of attention, trusting we will live up to the opportunity afforded to us.
I suppose it is optimistic to think that this motion is going to pass. It does not seem to be the usual habit in this House to pass motions between five and six o'clock. But I
574

October 21, 1974
Food and Resources
wish it would pass, because then the government would receive the message from parliament that we give the highest priority to the subject under discussion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON FOOD AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) has put before the House this afternoon a very important motion, one that concerns all of us, namely, the critical issue of world food supplies. There can be no doubt that the spectre of starvation and hunger on a massive scale now seems closer than it has been for many years or, perhaps, than it has ever been. Not only are we in Canada deeply concerned at the possible plight of millions in many parts of the globe; attention all over the world has become focussed on the world food crisis to an ever increasing degree.
No fewer than three international organizations have held, or will soon be holding meetings to review the urgent world food situation. From October 20 to 26, the intergovernmental committee of the World Food Program is holding its twenty-sixth session. From November 18 to November 29 the FAO Council will convene its 64th session in Rome. A few weeks ago the preparatory committee for the World Food Conference held its third session. And, of course, the most important event of all, the World Food Conference, will be held in Rome from November 5 to November 16. Canadians are involved in all these discussions and, indeed, there will be a high ranking Canadian delegation attending the World Food Conference. The minister indicated in the House a few weeks ago that he was considering attending the conference himself.
The hon. member for Egmont has mentioned some specific measures on this subject. He has suggested that all the countries of the world should report annually on their food resources and food needs, and he has put forward a formula for the transfer of these resources from the "have" to the "have not" countries.
Moreover, he has suggested that this House express itself as being in favour of establishing a new international organization to oversee these tasks, which he would call a "World Commission on Food and Resources". The hon. member has not been the only one to suggest an inventory of world food resources. Indeed, he is in the best of company. The draft International Undertaking on World Food Security endorsed by the FAO Council in July 1974- commonly known as the "Boerma Proposal"-has this to say:
The effective functioning of the world food security system will depend greatly on the availability of timely and adequate information.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you recognized me and I intend to put as many of my remarks on the record as possible. I

think the procedure is to move back and forth across the House, and that is exactly what we have done.
Let me return to the quotation as follows:
The effective functioning of the world food security system will depend greatly on the availability of timely and adequate information. Government members of FAO should furnish to the Director-General on a regular basis all the available information on national stock levels, government stockholding programs and policies, current and prospective export availabilities and import requirements for cereals, and relevant aspects of the supply and demand situation, as well as on assistance provided to the food production programs in developing countries. Other governments should be invited to provide similar information. In order to avoid unfavourable market repercussions in particular, the Director-General of FAO should ensure, where so requested by a government, that the data supplied by that government to the information system are made available on a restricted basis only to the governments adhering to the undertaking.
This report went on to say:
To keep all governments directly informed of current developments in the international cereals position during periods when world supplies are scarce the Director-General of FAO should prepare, on a quarterly basis or more frequently, concise factual appraisals of the situation and outlook which should be circulated promptly to governments.
It continued:
In the assembly and analysis of information and statistics, the Director-General of FAO should seek the assistance of the International Wheat Council and other intergovernmental organizations concerned.
At the same time the Japanese proposed that there be a global information system on the world food situation. Had there been such a system, according to this proposal it would have been possible to avoid, or at least to attenuate the grave situation which the world has recently experienced. In view of the uncertain prospects as regards food supplies, there is an urgent need for a more comprehensive and global information system.
The Japanese proposal continued as follows:
It is noted that one important function of FAO, IWC and other international organizations is the collection and analysis of worldwide information on food and agriculture. These existing information functions should be further improved and strengthened for the reasons set out above. The proposed information system is designed to enhance the usefulness of the information collected by the various existing institutions (FAO, IWC, WHO, etc.) through coordinating their information activities and thus making information available to this system and enabling it to compile such information in a comprehensive and integrated manner.
Acting on this proposal the preparatory committee for the World Food Conference agreed that there was an urgent need for establishing a worldwide food information system to strengthen the implementation of world food security and to promote marked stability in a constantly changing food and agricultural situation. It felt that the main features and objectives of the tow proposals were essentially similar and complementary, and that it was desirable to combine them. It was noted that the nucleus of a food information system already existed in FAO, and that other international organizations, such as the International Wheat Council, also collected useful information on food and agriculture.
There was support for building on these existing information arrangements. The global food information system should aim at identifying countries or regions where acute food shortages were likely to arise, at monitoring the
October 21, 1974

world food supply-demand situation in order to help governments to take prompt measures, and at contributing to the efficient working of the proposed international undertaking on world food security.
The committee felt that the food information system should also assemble, analyse and disseminate comprehensive and timely information on the situation and prospects of main crops and livestocks products, export availabilities and import requirements, supplies of agricultural requisites, particularly fertilizers and weather conditions, including, as far as possible, forecasts. Many delegates stressed that full and active participation in the information system by all countries, particularly those which were major producers, consumers and or traders, was essential for the effective functioning of the system. The committee recognized that technical assistance would be required to build up national food information services in developing countries. Several delegates stressed that some of the information provided by governments might be sensitive and would need to be used with care and discretion so as to avoid speculative activities which would disturb the markets.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Buchanan that Bill C-15 respecting oil and gas in Indian lands, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know the minister wishes the bill to receive second reading and to move on to the next stage so I shall bring my remarks directly to the point.
Before I begin my few observations I wish the minister would remember what the honourable member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) was saying because he was enunciating a very simple economic truth, namely, that we all hope the Indian bands will be fortunate in finding oil or gas underneath their reservation lands, but that possibility would not exist unless there is a viable drilling industry available to do the work. This is all part of the wider oil and gas play. I shall not say more about this because the economic truth of it is self-evident.
The two points about which I wish to speak are covered by phrases which may be strange to the minister but I hope will not remain strange too long. I refer first to
Indian Affairs
front-end loading, and secondly to the technique of sharing with the Indians. Front-end loading is a device that has cost the Canadian people very dearly in connection with their resource industries, particularly oil and gas.
Front-end loading is simply the natural desire of a provincial or federal government to obtain as much in tax revenue as possible out of industry at the very beginning, even though it can be shown quantitatively that if the provincial and/or the federal government were to lay off that industry in the years of its capital pay-out there would be more money for the people on whose land the oil or gas well is situated, and also more money for the provincial and federal governments.
To put it very simply, if one examines the history of the oil and gas pools of western Canada one will find, say, a typical oil pool with X number of barrels in it whose capital cost of development would run between $600 million and $900 million. Of that amount of $600 million to $900 million, an amount of $400 million to $700 million would have been in the form of front-end loading charges imposed on that industry by greedy governments trying to pluck the goose before it was ready to lay the egg.
Another way of putting it is that the resource industries, including oil and gas, are capital intensive, and the larger amount of the dollars required to handle the development of those industries is the capital cost. So, if governments could hold off in respect of the front-end loading charges, and made certain a company received no money out of it either until the capital costs were repaid, there would be more money for all those wishing to participate in the revenue or rent from the resource being developed.
The principle of front-end loading has been traditional on the United States oil and gas scene for many years. In Canada we have copied the United States system. We have front-end loaded our industry. The only winners when companies have to borrow all this capital are the money lenders because the individual company has the longer period of pay-out. It is being milked when it should be devoting all its revenue toward paying back the capital cost.
Front-end loading takes the form of lease fees, permit fees and those wonderful "bonus payments." Every time the government thinks it is doing a wonderful job, it actually is destroying the capability of oil fields to pay an extra dividend to the owners. I shall not say much more than that, except that in the federal oil and gas regulations as applied to federal lands, when first published in 1961, there was a government in Canada which did without this front-end loading and said to the oil gas companies that it would not charge them anything.
Then the government said that in return for not charging them anything at the permit or exploration stage, when the lease stage-which is the ownership stage-was reached, the government wanted two things. The first was Canadian ownership of the developing company. This can be found in the federal regulations dealing with all lands except Indian lands. I ask the minister to consider that as an option which he should have in the regulations he promulgates for the handling of oil, gas and minerals on the reservations. He will find those provisions are very fair.
28305-37l/a

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
Secondly the government of 1961 said to the oil and gas companies that when they explored in territories and offshore, since all the front-end loading had been taken off, instead of getting 12 per cent, 13 per cent or 17 per cent royalty the government wanted something in the order of 60 per cent. The government said that, and got it. If you take the heavy load of paying for the big capital input off the shoulders of companies in the early stage then, when the capital input is paid off, they are well able to pay these higher royalties. It can be proven quantitatively that they get more money out of their investment, and the owners of the oil resource, the people of Canada, and in this case the Indians, will get more.
I am not giving the minister a great Sunday school lecture on something we did that is good. I am simply saying our history shows that in the provinces we did something that was bad and we are paying heavily for it today. The federal government in 1961 tried to do something more moderate and good, but we have not had the big finds that would quantitively demonstrate how, if it had followed those regulations through, the people of Canada would have got much more out of them percentagewise than out of the front end loading technique.
I hope the minister will forgive me for having gone over this bit of history, but he is looking at a person who stayed out in the wilderness for many years and watched this debauchery and robbery of our resources. This was not done so much by the companies as by the moneylenders who got control and, over the long period that the loans were being paid back, got the greater bulk of the value of the oil and gas into their own hands instead it going into the hands of the entrepreneurs, and particularly of those people who owned the oil and gas reserves.
This is the crime committed in the last 25 years against the people of Canada, mostly in the lands that belong to the provinces. Now we have a chance in our northern lands, our offshore areas, and on Indian lands that are under federal control within the provinces, to avoid that mistake. I would ask the minister to read the original regulations and he will find the philosophy and principles are sound. I could of course suggest several modifications today that would allow for new developments. To my knowledge there is only one person in the public service of Canada today who understands that philosophy. He helped me draft the regulations, and I think it would be worth the minister's while to search for him. He is now at a high level in a different department.
This second point is probably the most difficult moral problem of all. The lands we gave the Indians were theirs to enjoy all the fruits of those lands, whether rabbits, grouse, oil, gas or minerals. That was a moral commitment by those who took the lands from our first Canadians, in effect, by force. They were guaranteed that as long as the moon shone and rivers flowed, the land was theirs. The oil, gas and minerals mentioned in the legislation do not belong to the people of Canada-they belong to the Indians-period. The minister is the only person who can protect the Indian ownership of wealth inside the reservations.

The problem will be more difficult in the territories because of the lack of treaties and reservations. I would hope, however, that any government response to the moral obligation that our grandfathers made in giving the land and the reservations to the treaty Indians would realize that the same principle, in some modified measure, has to be applied to the non-treaty Indians. If the minister is to act as trustee he would be wise to hold down the front end loading so that in the end there will be more money to go to the Indians themselves.
These are non-renewable capital resources that will last only another 15 or 30 years, depending on whether they be oil or gas, depending on all the physical conditions that make a reservoir or mining deposit. According to the experience of our predecessors, when you are selling your capital, that capital should not be considered as income but as capital wealth to be invested. The only money that should go to the Indians in trust is income from the capital fund. It will probably be 15 or 20 years before the resource is depleted completely, and the revenue collected in that time should make a rather large fund. The income from that fund in perpetuity would be very important to future generations on the reservations.
There are many precedents for this, Madam Speaker. In the provinces governments sold off land for school purposes. In the prairies, two sections out of 36 were set aside for education. The money was put into trust funds and the educational system-certainly in the thirties-was financed almost entirely by revenue from those capital funds. Government after government in the three prairie provinces followed this practice, and none has betrayed what was done there over 70 years ago. These school land trust funds are still providing money for the educational system.
I think it is fair to say, that over the years all political parties in this House have acknowledged that we are guilty of great crimes against our first citizens. We must begin to correct those crimes committed in the name of expansion and advance. All political parties would, I am sure, support this.
All past ministers in charge of Indian Affairs in this House received support from all parts of the House because they all wanted to do the right thing for the Indians. This is still the case, and I am sure in this debate the minister has sensed a willingness to support this measure. We all know his difficulties which are almost beyond human solution. Although his predecessors tried to the limit of their strength and ability to resolve the problems, they are still there. Hopefully we can come closer to bringing justice to our first citizens, without being sentimental about it, but being realistically and morally proper. I hope these ideas strike the minister as worth while, and that he will take them under consideration.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to contribute a few remarks this evening on the bill before the House. I represent a constituency that has a variety of Indian reservations in it, but as yet neither oil nor gas has been discovered there to my knowledge. But one never knows what might happen, with continued searches and continued fuel shortages.
October 21, 1974

As I read the bill I was reminded of an experience I had when first elected to this House. A very elderly mining engineer who was interested in developing a mining property spoke to me in highest terms of its possibilities. It sounded like something to gladden the heart but there was just one drawback; it was sited within an Indian reservation on Indian land. After listening to his glowing description I wondered why it had not been developed up to that point. I investigated, and came across the agreement that had been signed by the province of British Columbia and the federal government regarding mining development on Indian lands in British Columbia. It was easy then to see why no reservation in British Columbia would be wildly excited about having anyone develop a mining property. At that time Indians seemed to lose effective control of anything below the surface of the land the moment development started.
As I read the bill some questions came to my mind. On page 2, clause 4(b) reads:
The Governor in Council may make regulations
(b) respecting the disposition of any interest in Indian lands necessarily incidental to the exploitation of oil and gas in such lands and the terms and conditions thereof;
That sounds heavy handed. I sometimes wonder why those who draft government bills use such language. It seems to me that this bill is lacking in specific reference to the Indian peoples. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has already pointed out that clause 5(2) contains the only reference to band council. I wonder why clause 4 did not provide for some specific role for band councils. Why is it worded in language which suggests the federal government alone can make dispositions which it feels desirable with regard to oil and gas on Indian reservations?
I know that those preparing a bill always say, "Of course, this is the legal way of preparing it, but it will be interpreted differently". We find over and over again that, once a bill becomes law, it is interpreted sometimes in a startlingly legal and narrow way, and not as it was suggested it would be interpreted. I hope that will not happen here.
If I were a member of an Indian band who suspected there might be oil or gas on my reservation, I would be concerned about the wording of this bill. I also wonder about the complexities in distinguishing private ownership and band ownership of land on Indian reservations. This bill does not deal with this sensitive area. It does not sort out who has control and jurisdiction on reservations in this matter.
I hope that during committee study of this bill we will hear from a large variety of people, and from those representing the Indian bands themselves. I hope we will not see a repetition of what happened in the committee studying grain handling problems, when we heard only the minister. It is essential that the parliamentary committee studying this bill hear from a wide variety of interested people.
Indian Affairs
Nor does the bill spell out the disposition of royalties which, if this bill becomes law, we anticipate will accrue to the Indian peoples.
I am concerned about the timing of the bill. Actually, it involves two sensitive issues, royalties from natural resource production-and this in British Columbia and other provinces has been a sensitive area-and federal interference with regard to Indian lands, even though they have been set aside as reservations under treaty. So, here are two sensitive issues. There is little in the bill to suggest that the government, in preparing it, has been as sensitive, cautious and thoughtful on these two issues as it might have been, and as our treatment of the native peoples of Canada warrants.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LEASES, LICENCES AND ROYALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief. I shall comment about points raised by some hon. members opposite.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) referred to the question of the Indian people assuming greater economic control, and gaining the economic advantage which would flow to them from the type of development referred to in the bill. His was an interesting thought.
In this connection may I refer to the recent announcement in the newspapers concerning the very large development of the Enoch band in the west end of Edmonton. They are in favour of the large developments referred to, the precise reason being that the 30 oil wells and three gas wells will probably run dry around 1980. They intend to use these resources in order to create an alternate economic base, as they will gradually lose the benefit of their present resource in the next 10 or 15 years. More activity like this is going on among the Indian people. Such activity ties in with what was said by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who spoke about the use of funds to develop a significant base for the Indian people.
Other members, the hon. member for Peace River, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone), the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) and, lastly, the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston), referred to the broad nature of the bill. They were concerned because it is not precisely worded. I emphasize that the bill was drafted this way so that we shall not lock ourselves into the tight process envisaged under earlier arrangements which did not provide for flexibility in changing or altering royalty arrangements. That, really, is why the bill has been drafted this way. We want to respond to situations quickly, as they arise, rather than find ourselves locked into a relatively inflexible situation.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich did not like the word surrender. I share his feeling and am concerned about the word every time I see it in connection with Indian lands. I, also, would prefer a word alternative to surrender, if we become involved in leasing situations.

October 21, 1974
Indian Affairs
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) expressed concern which was shared by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain about the deductibility of royalites.
