maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
that Bill C-4, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act and Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is again my privilege to be speaking on a bill which will further improve the quality of life of that particular group of citizens whose service earned them the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act or Part XI of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act.
The bill before you, like Bill C-148 introduced last year, is especially important because it is also breaking new ground in the field of veterans legislation. You will remember that Bill C-148 abolished, for the first time in the history of the War Veterans Allowance Act, the ceiling on personal property. This Bill, C-4, is equally or possibly more important because it will provide, for the first time in the 44 year life of this valuable legislation, for the

payment of additional moneys for recipients with dependent children.
Up until now the only benefit that has existed for children, other than orphans, has been the provision whereby a widow or widower with a child would receive the allowance at the married rate. Unfortunately, however, the money paid was the same if the widow or widower had one child or six.
The legislation also failed to face that fact that a married veteran with a child needed more money than a married veteran with no children. Bill C-4 recognizes this fact by providing an additional $50, less the amount of family allowances in pay, for each child. I am especially pleased with this improvement, because it has troubled me for some time that we did not provide more adequately for children under these acts. This situation will be corrected by the passage of this bill.
The bill, I am glad to state, also makes more generous provision for our orphan. In place of the old descending scale of $91.95 for one, $161.27 for two, $217.24 for three or more, with no more dollars being paid for five orphans than for three, we now propose a flat rate of $125 per month, less the amount of family allowance in pay, with a monthly income ceiling of $135.95 for each orphan regardless of the number. These new rates and ceilings for orphans will be escalated annually. We also propose that the allowance to an orphan, or on behalf of a child, be continued to age 25 as long as the child continues his education. The present act requires payments normally to stop at age 21.
In addition to the new benefits for children and the improved payments for orphans, this bill also provides for the WVA/CWA income ceiling to be escalated by 5.3 per cent effective October 1, 1973, and the rates by similar dollar amounts. It provides for the quarterly escalation of ceilings in accordance with the increase in the cost of living, except for orphans whose income ceilings and rates will continue to be escalated annually. This method of escalating on the ceiling instead of on the rate will give the WVA/CWA recipient the advantage of an escalation on a larger base.
The escalation I have just referred to, effective October 1, 1973, will require the adjustment of over 80,000 accounts, and I am confident that all members of this House will agree and understand that if these amendments are passed by parliament there will be a period of time required before these can be reflected in the cheques of our recipients. I assure, you, however, that everything will be done to adjust the accounts with the least possible delay so that our recipients will benefit as soon as possible from any increase parliament approves.
If this bill is passed, the end result will be that effective October, 1 1974, a single recipient will have an average monthly income ceiling of $223.66 and may, depending on other income, receive an allowance of up to $183.66 per month. In the case of a married recipient the average monthly income ceiling will be $382.90 and the allowance payable, depending on other income, will be raised to a maximum, of $312.90 per month. The ceilings will be escalated quarterly in accordance with the cost of living increase and the rates increased by similar amounts.
October 21, 1974

Effective April 1, 1974, the allowance will continue on behalf of an eligible child or orphan up to age 25 years as long as he continues with his studies. Also effective April 1, 1974, the rates for orphans will be increased to $125 per month, less the amount of family allowance in pay, with an income ceiling of $135.95, the ceiling to be escalated annually in accordance with the cost of living, and the rates to be increased by a like dollar amount.
Effective October 1, 1974, we will provide an additional $50 a month for each child, less family allowance, with the result that a man, wife and one child will have an income ceiling of $432.90, and a possible monthly allowance of $362.90. This ceiling will be increased quarterly in accordance with the cost of living index, and the rate will be increased by a similar dollar amount. In cases of proven need the assistance fund can be used to bring the income level up to the ceiling, $432.90.
The situation will be slightly different in the case of the widow or widower with one child in that the additional $50 will not be paid because they will continue to receive the more beneficial married rate and to have the advantage of the married income ceiling as at present. In this instance, because the additional $50 is not being paid, family allowances will not be taken into consideration. As of October 1, 1974 this group will have an average monthly income ceiling of $382.90 and a monthly rate, depending on other income, of up to $312.90.
In addition to the points I have referred to, I am also pleased that this bill contains several proposals in line with the government's policy to provide equality of status for men and women.
I am proud of the record of this government, and indeed of this House, for the way in which they have treated our veterans and their dependents. I am confident that members of all parties will see Bill C-4 as I do, as another step forward in the field of veterans legislation, a field in which Canada is a proud leader.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is significant that as a result of the amendments in this bill, Canada and parliament are taking a first step in equality for males and females with regard to veterans legislation, when Madam Speaker is in the Chair for the first time.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
I have studied the bill. I can only say that the amendments are commendable. My party has no quarrel with the contents of the bill except for one or two reservations which I hope to deal with a little later. I must say that we in this party are pleased that most of the amendments seem to be related very closely to the program for veterans affairs that was produced by my party as a policy prior to the July 8 election.
I am glad our party was of some help to the minister and to the Department of Veterans Affairs in producing a bill which will overcome many of the inequities which have existed over the years, subject to the reservations I mentioned earlier. As is customary, the amendments were brought about in consultation with the veterans organiza-
Veterans Affairs
tions of Canada. We owe a tribute to the National Council of Veterans Organizations which, over the years, has made representations on behalf of its membership. It is through the Council's efforts that many of these amendments are being put into effect. I feel a tribute is owed as well to the Woods committee which, four or five years ago, carried out a comprehensive study concerning the status of veterans. I am sure the efforts made by that committee, and the advice it gave, were instrumental in bringing about some of the excellent amendments contained in this bill.
As I have said many times in the past, a good deal of the progress in veterans legislation results from the fact that many of the people who serve in the various agencies in the Department of Veterans Affairs are themselves veterans. Not only do they perform their duties with capability but they do so with dedication. They, too, served their country in time of need, side by side with their comrades to whom they now administer.
Since we are dealing tonight with war veterans allowances I should like to mention the War Veterances Allowance Board, particularly the chairman, Mr. Don Thompson, his staff, and the district authorities across the country who have served the veterans so well. Mr. Thompson served most of the post war years as dominion secretary of the Dominion Command of the Royal Canadian Legion. In the past few years he has been chairman of the War Veterans Allowances Board and, although he is not in the gallery tonight-

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext: He is.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
-I feel he deserves a special tribute. If he is here I hope I am not embarrassing him. We owe a tribute to Don Thompson and his staff for helping to bring about many of the amendments we see in Bill C-4.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is a little different from other departments of government in that the majority of the staff are veterans and know the problems of veterans. I am sure they are dedicated to the progress of the legislation which comes before us, and I feel this shows a good hope for Canada. I might say of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs that it, too, is a little different from the other committees of the House of Commons. We try to deal with our business on a non partisan basis.
Unfortunately, perhaps, there is no sex appeal in veterans affairs to attract the attention of the press. It is rarely that controversial matters come up for consideration. Nevertheless, I respectfully request the people in the Press Gallery tonight to make known the contents of this bill to all veterans, so that they may take advantage of these benefits and learn what we are trying to do for them.
I can only add that there may be a change in the non-partisan nature of the Veterans Affairs Committee if the minister does not agree with the representations we have made from this side of the House with regard to the Veterans Land Act. However, there is still a ray of hope. In reply to a question I put to him-if I may refer to our proceedings last week-the minister indicated that a departmental committee is now working on some type of housing program for veterans. I hope this will come about and that we can continue to serve veterans as they deserve.

October 21, 1974
Veterans Affairs
In any case, through an amendment put down by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to the Veterans Land Act measure, extending the expiry date, we shall soon have an opportunity to debate this situation. I hope the government will recognize that we cannot in any circumstances phase out the Veterans Land Act which provides a housing program and accommodation for many veterans who deserve this program because they served Canada in time of need.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext: We should improve it.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend says we should improve it. I must say that the policy paper adopted by my party sets out five or six points which would improve the legislation. I hope the minister will do more than simply tell me in the House that he will consider these proposals. I hope he will take the necessary action. I know he wishes to do so; now he has to convince his colleagues in the cabinet some of whom have lost consideration for our veterans, something it is so easy to do between world wars.
As I have said, the bill is a good one. It will overcome many of the inequities which presently exist and, to a large extent, it will allow veterans to meet the increased cost of living. Moreover, it is one of the first steps toward giving equality of status between males and females, one of the most important portions of the program which our party produced prior to the July election.
The bill embodies at least 12 important amendments. It provides entitlement for widowers who have reached the age of 60, special awards to a surviving spouse with respect to dependent children; for changes in the determination of allowances payable to veterans married to each other; for allowances to a widow who is maintaining a veteran or a person in receipt of civilian war allowance, and revises from 21 to 25 years the age until which a child may receive an allowance while following an approved course of instruction. This is very important because, as we all know, under the present act the dependent child of a veteran could attend university until the age of 21. Naturally, this does not suit the purpose because students continue at university until at least the age of 25. This measure will provide them with the assistance that they need.
Another important point which was in our policy paper is that the bill will provide for quarterly adjustments of the income factor, another step in the right direction. The only legislation that provided for this was the old Age Security Act. As this session progresses I hope this criterion will be used to provide quarterly indexing of disability pensions. I know the minister is considering this, and I hope he will be able to persuade the cabinet to provide quarterly indexing for disabled pensioners who suffer from increase in the cost of living.
The bill also provides for new allowances for dependent children. I mention these improvements generally at this time since we wish to co-operate in getting through the second stage of the bill. However, we will deal with the bill clause by clause at committee stage.
One of the important features of the bill, unless I am mistaken, is that no longer will the value of the home of a

recipient and the determination of his amount of income restrict him or her from receiving the war veterans allowance.
However, in spite of the dozen or so amendments that will overcome many of the inequities that exist in the act, I feel that we, as parliamentarians, should not feel too proud of the fact that it has taken so long, some 44 years since the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act were passed, to reach this stage. Having reached this stage, there still remain some inequities that must be eliminated. We should give the veterans of Canada legislation that does not have to be amended every year at the political whim of the government so that we can finally care for our burnt out veterans.
It should forever remain on the consciences of past and present parliamentarians that too many veterans over the years have passed on, having been disappointed and discouraged that Canada failed to live up to its commitment to those who served and to whom we should have shown a little more compassion and consideration. Regardless of which side of the House we sit on, we in this parliament should demand a veterans charter that will provide, to our remaining veterans and their dependents, a reasonable pension that will give them adequate shelter.
One of the things I am sorry not to see in the bill is the elimination of the requirement for pension of 365 days' service in the United Kingdom before November 12, 1918, for first world war veterans. This would be a very simple amendment, one that has been introduced in this House of Commons over the years. I have before me a copy of a bill introduced by a colleague of mine, the former member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, Mr. McIntosh. This bill provided for a pension to veterans who did not serve for 365 days, payable on a pro rata basis. I should like to read the explanatory notes to this bill which was introducted in 1963:
The purpose of this Bill is to grant eligibility for an allowance under the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952 to those veterans of World War I who would qualify for an allowance except that they served in the United Kingdom less than 365 days prior to November 12th, 1918. The allowance, however, would be less than a standard allowance as it would be calculated on the fraction of the number of days served in fact (e.g., 200) divided by 365.
Since there are not too many veterans who fall into this category, there is no reason for not introducing such an amendment now. I might mention that the average age of first world war veterans is very close to 80, so how many years have they left? Some served in the United Kingdom for 360, even 361 days, so why cannot we fulfil our obligation to those who have only a few remaining years left to live and who could receive a little extra comfort?
A single recipient of old age security and the GIS today receives $199.10. According to the minister's statement which he distributed on October 2, as of September 30, 1973, a single recipient had a monthly income ceiling of $191.14. The new monthly income ceiling effective October 1, 1974, will be $223.66, reflecting a 17 per cent increase, or some $32.52. If we take into consideration the exemption for the war veteran over 65, all we are doing is providing him with $40 to $50 to give him a little extra comfort and allow him to cope with the increase in the cost of living that is so serious today.
October 21, 1974

Another inequity that should be overcome concerns those veterans of Canada who remained overseas and thus do not qualify for war veterans allowance owing to the provision that they must reside in Canada for 365 days. The minister is aware of this situation and has met these veterans over in England, as have his predecessors. The legislation of 1960 was amended to permit continuing payment of the allowance outside Canada primarily for the benefit of recipients who were desirous of leaving Canada for reasons of health or family ties. Apparently, 683 recipients have benefitted by this 1960 amendment, and I give credit to whoever was in power at that time.
Again it is surely not too much to ask that an amendment be passed to eliminate the 12 months' residence requirement in the case of the few Canadian veterans who are unable to draw the allowance because of their inability to return to Canada to qualify. If the reason for the amendment in 1960 permitting continuing payment of the allowance outside Canada was primarily for the benefit of recipients desirous of leaving Canada for reasons of health or family ties, then surely it is only fair that the converse should be applied, namely, that those veterans who are unable to return to reside in Canada for 12 months, for reasons of health or family ties, should be allowed the privilege of drawing the allowance without the necessity of having to return to Canada?
Many of these veterans are invalids and they cannot return to Canada. We are an affluent nation, and although I realize we must restrict government spending, there are many areas where we could save a lot of money by cutting out government waste. This would enable us to provide these Canadians with the extra comforts that they deserve, and we would be able to say that Canada has fulfilled its obligations to them for the service that they have given to their country.
We could also improve the act under regulation so as to increase the amount of casual earnings that a war veterans allowance recipient can receive. At present it is $1,000 for a single recipient and $1,500 for a married couple. In many cases the children of second world war veterans have grown up and gone their own way, and the wife is in a position to work and provide a little of the extras for herself and her husband. But she cannot do so because of the restrictions. I am sure this is a matter the minister will consider should be the subject of consultation between himself and his department in order that the amount of casual earnings allowed can be increased. Certainly that is something to be considered for the future.
I should like to make another point regarding the recipients of war veterans allowance who happen to have large families and, perhaps regrettably, qualify for social assistance in addition to the war veterans allowance. Whenever there is an increase in the war veterans allowance, that is, each January, in relation to the cost of living index, the social assistance is decreased. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is not in the House to hear this. Consultations should take place with the provinces regarding a change which will allow these veterans to receive the increased war veterans allowance without a decrease in social assistance.
Veterans Affairs
As the situation now stands, any increase in war veterans allowance is offset by a reduction in provincial social assistance. The same is true in respect of disability pensions. When a recipient of a war veterans allowance receives a partial increase in his disability pension there is corresponding decrease in his other allowance. With the various changes in disability pensions and war veterans allowances I hope this situation will be corrected.
Speaking on behalf of my colleagues, and particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think I can safely say we all want this bill to go the the committee as soon as possible in order that it can be returned to this House and be passed here. A lot of administration is involved in getting payments out. A great deal of administration is involved in quarterly indexing, as well as in respect of other factors in the bill. I can only say that we commend the minister wholeheartedly for his introduction of this amendment. I hope he will consider the amendments to which I have referred. If he does not, it is my intention to suggest such changes at the committee stage. I am sure that with a little effort we could bring in amendments to make the war veterans allowance bill a complete legislative item to serve the war veteran and burnt out veterans for years, without the necessity of having to come back each year to agree to ad hoc amendments.
I again commend the minister and the government on this bill. I look forward to its speedy passage in committee and its return to this House so that it can be passed for the benefit of those veterans of Canada who have served so well over the years.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say "Madam Speaker" fast before the Chair becomes Mr. Speaker. In any case, as a first word I want to say on behalf of my party that we warmly welcome Bill C-4. Like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), we want to expedite the passing of this bill so it will be in effect just as soon as possible.
It is quite true that before I conclude my remarks I shall play the role of an opposition member, indicating a few things that are wrong, or pointing out a few shortcomings. But my main feeling about this bill is that it is good. It has more things in it I can praise than if often the case. One has difficulty in finding the jokers that are so frequently in bills the government brings forward.
I want also to join with my friend and colleagues, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, in paying certain tributes. I was aware of the fact that while he was doing so he, as a member from Newfoundland, was telling the minister, who is a representative from Prince Edward Island, what a good war veterans allowance board chairman he has, who happens to come from New Brunswick. I suppose I could fall back on my Nova Scotia background and make this an Atlantic provinces night.
In any event I want to join in the tribute to Mr. Donald Thompson and his staff for the good work they do in administering the War Veterans Allowance Act. As the hon. member says, we pay the same tribute to other officials in the Department of Veterans Affairs, but tonight what we have before us is the War Veterans Allowance Act.
582

October 21, 1974
Veterans Affairs
As I said, there are a number of things about the amendments presented tonight that are good. Let me take a few minutes to emphasize them, even though they have already been noted.
This bill is good in that it establishes equality between the sexes so far as veterans under his legislation are concerned. I suppose this equality of sexes is demonstrated by the fact that when I started my remarks it was Madam Speaker but there has been a change and now it is Mr. Speaker in the Chair. There is, of course, still a slight difference. I suppose "vive la difference" will always be the motto, and there will always be some differences between the sexes.
I notice under the provisions of this bill that, although a male veteran can make it possible for his widow to draw the war veterans allowance at age 55, the female veteran can make it possible for her widower to draw it only when he reaches 60. I suppose the difference is that not many women admit to getting past 55, but at any rate that slight difference still seems to exist.
In any case the provisions of the bill as I read it seem to establish equality between male and female veterans, and the bill also makes special provisions where a male and female veteran are married to each other. We welcome these changes. They are indeed in line with other changes being made in a number of our federal statutes.
The second thing about this bill I feel to be particularly good is the one the minister referred to in the opening portion of his remarks, namely, the provision which is made for an extra payment in the case of children. As he pointed out, the only way a child received anything before was in the case of a parent of single status getting the married rate if that parent was maintaining a child or children. Now, under the provisions of this bill, the children of war veterans allowance recipients up to a certain age are to be provided in their own right, with the amounts set out in the legislation.
Before I leave this I must say I am not happy about the provision that subtracts from the amount being paid in respect of a child the amount received as a family allowance. It seems to me this is a case of the old means test concept taking a long time to die out.
I remind the minister that the War Veterans Allowance Board has already found it possible in other areas to exempt certain forms of income. For example, even though the war veterans allowance is tied into the guaranteed income supplement that goes with old age security, the War Veterans Allowance Board by Order in Council exempts the escalation of old age security and the guaranteed income supplement. I believe there have been also arrangements between the War Veterans Allowance Board and my province of Manitoba, where a mincome program is being established, to make it clear that money received under that program will not count as income for purposes of the war veterans allowance.
There are other examples of this. The point I am making, however, is that it has been found possible to exempt certain other forms of income from the means or income test that attaches to the war veterans allowance. I contend that this could be done in respect of the family

allowance. I just do not think it stands up for us to embark on this new idea of providing, under the War Veterans Allowance Act, something for the children of war veterans allowance recipients and then to turn right around and take away with one hand what is given with the other. I realize the defence which can be put up in this regard and no doubt we will face that in committee, but it seems we are back to square one on this business, and that it is time to mix in the means test on these payments to which these children are entitled.
I come to the third item in the bill which I regard as good. I shall do my best to avoid any criticism of it because it is something for which I have been asking for a long time. We have it now and I want to say that it is most welcome. I refer to the decision to escalate the ceiling rather than the allowance. That is saying it in shorthand, despite the fact that it is rather complicated.
Up until the present time the way the government has worked has been to increase the maximum allowance payable by the percentage increase in the cost of living, and then raise the ceiling on permissible income only by the same number of dollars that the allowance was raised. That meant that the ceiling on the permissible income applied to the war veterans allowance did not go up by the percentage increase in the cost of living.
I argued all along that the escalation should apply to the ceiling rather than to the allowance. That is now being done in this bill and I think it is one of the most important changes being made. From now on the escalation is on the total income allowed to a war veterans allowance recipient. That ceiling will be escalated by the actual rise in the cost of living, and the allowance will be increased by the number of dollars necessary to keep the allowance the same number of dollars below the ceiling. As I say this is something some of us have been pressing for, for a long time. Now it is here and we welcome it very warmly.
I wish also to express approval of the fact that the escalation under the War Veterans Allowance Act, once this bill comes into effect, will be on a quarterly rather than on an annual basis. Ever since the old age security and the guaranteed income supplement were placed on a quarterly basis that has been a bone of contention with war veterans allowance recipients and others. They could not understand why they were not put on the same basis. This is being done and we welcome it.
I go further and say, if I understand the bill-and I have tried to read it with a view to grasping it-that there will be retroactive payments. The minister's statement tonight about 80,000 accounts having to be adjusted seems to confirm that. It is also confirmed by the fact that the various schedules in the bill indicate the rates of ceiling and rates of allowance for each of the quarters in the current year.
Therefore, it looks as though there will be a case of retroactivity in respect of a war veterans allowance recipient over these past number of months. In other words, we are adopting the idea that the escalation should have applied to the ceiling since last October, and the adjustments will be made on that basis. That is good.
I hope the computers in the department are in good working order and that it will not take too long for these
October 21, 1974

80,000	accounts to be adjusted. Everyone recognizes that it will take some time, but we hear of computers which, if they are fed the necessary information, can pass out so many hundreds of results per second. I hope these adjustments can be made soon and that all those in receipt of war veterans allowance will obtain the benefit of the new formula without delay.
That is not an inconsiderable list of things to find in a bill which one has to say are good. They are all very good and they are welcome. That leads me to draw attention to some shortcomings and some things which are not here at all. In respect of the point I have been discussing about quarterly escalation I still regret-and we will run into this as time goes on-that the plan of escalation is one that is always behind.
The plan being adopted for war veterans allowance escalation is exactly the same plan as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) brought in with respect to old age security and the quaranteed income supplement. So, I cannot ask one minister to do something without asking the other minister to do the same thing. Since both are present this evening I put this to both of them.
The plan that is in this bill, like the plan applying to OAS and GIS, works this way. At the beginning of a quarter you go back two months. Then you take the three months prior to those two months, and you compare the cost of living in those three months with the three months prior thereto. So when you have an escalation in the allowance or an escalation in old age security and the guaranteed income supplement you are really eight months behind. To tell me this is because it is too complicated to compute is something I cannot swallow.
Then in respect of the orphans, the orphans' benefits will not escalate quarterly but rather annually. Again the minister has been handed the program that is in the legislation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. When you get an escalation in January you go back three months, take the 12 months before that and compare the cost of living in that 12 months with the 12 months before that. The time when people need the escalation most is when the cost of living has gone up, and not eight months later as in the quarterly case, or a couple of years later as is almost the case in the instance of annual escalation.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare receives many letters complaining about the escalation of old age pensions being behind. The Minister of Veterans Affairs will soon get the same treatment. He is hoping that all he is going to get will be many letters thanking him for this escalation on a quarterly basis. He will get those, but it will not be long until letters come saying that it is very nice to get the escalation but it is not enough, that it does not match the rise in the cost of living and that it is five or six months out of date.
I therefore urge the minister to get interested in this subject and have a conference with the Minister of National Health and Welfare so that they may soon come up with an idea on escalation that is more up to date than this scheme which is patterned after the one in the Old Age Security Act, with all of its shortcomings.
Veterans Affairs
Speaking of escalation, I want to support the proposal made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe that it ought also now to apply to disability pensions. It seems to me there are going to be all sorts of complications with old age security, the guaranteed income supplement and the war veterans allowance being escalated quarterly, and the war disability pension being escalated annually.
The minister shakes his head, Mr. Speaker. I do not know whether he was worrying about those complications or saying, in effect, "No matter what we do those fellows over there want something more". It is this government that boasts about quarterly escalation and that it brought it in for old age pensions and for the guaranteed income supplement, after the Minister of National Health and Welfare said he did not want to do that but would rather bring in substantial increases in the basic amount. Well, the government cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker; if it is proud of having brought in quarterly escalation for a number of programs, the onus is on the government to bring it in for all pension programs.
To return to the War Veterans Allowances Act, I listened with interest when my friend from Newfoundland said he could not read his notes. I thought he was looking down here and reading mine because I have only one point noted that he did not have. He was perfectly right in his plea about the 365 day requirement. I understood this requirement when it was put in the War Veterans Allowance Act over 40 years ago. This applies to veterans of World War I.
Surely we do not need any longer to deny veterans aged 75, 80 or 85 the benefit of the war veterans allowance because their service in England in world war I was only 364, 360 or even only 180 days? It seems to me that at this point we could say to a veteran who saw any service at all overseas in World War I that he can qualify for the war veterans allowance.
I liked the way the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe was putting it, Mr. Speaker. He did not use the words "guaranteed annual income for veterans" but that is what he was advocating. I suggest the time has come when we ought to say to any veteran of World War I that he does not any longer have to go through the rigmarole necessary under the Canadian Pension Commission, or to meet the tests of the war veterans allowance board, but rather that a guaranteed annual income will be his by right.
Someone will immediately suggest that there are veterans of World War II who are just as old. All right, we could establish the age at 75, 70 or 65 and say to every veteran in the country that at that age he is to be guaranteed an annual income. As the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe has proposed, it should be reasonably better than the income provided under our civilian social security legislation. It is a good place to begin this concept of a guaranteed annual income and I strongly urge it upon the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
I said that I had one point that the hon. member for Humber-St-George's-St. Barbe did not see when he looked over here, Mr. Speaker. It relates to the war disability pensions paid under the Pension Act but it has a tie-in with the War Veterans Allowance Act. I have in mind the
28305-381/!

October 21, 1974
Veterans Affairs
provision which denies the widow of any veteran a war widow's pension unless her husband was on a disability pension of 48 per cent or more before he died. The Woods commission recommended that this should be scrapped in favour of a pro rata arrangement, and that any widow of a veteran who had had a disability pension should get a pension as of right, whatever the scale might be. I think we should start to apply that to widows, especially widows of veterans of World War I. I welcome the sympathetic hearing that has been given this matter by the minister and various officials in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. I just hope that this year we get somewhere with this idea.
As the last speaker said, there will be an opportunity some time soon to discuss the War Veterans Land Act so we need not go into that tonight. The notice under the amendment to the statute of last spring was filed last Thursday, October 17, so that means that within 15 days we get to that debate-that is, Mr. Speaker, unless the minister beats us to it one of these days by announcing a new veterans housing program. I would be quite happy if he were to do so.
What we have before us tonight is the War Veterans Allowance Act and I say again that we welcome the improvements being made. I hope the minister will become part of an effort to get escalation more up to date. I hope he will take another look at the matter of applying a family allowance test to the moneys to be made available to the children of war veterans allowance recipients. I hope he will get rid of that 365 day clause for veterans of World War I and I hope he will take a new look at the position of all widows, especially those whose husbands were on pensions of less than 48 per cent before they died.
I have no quarrel at all with the minister's pride in presenting this legislation. As a package it is one of the best sets of improvements in the War Veterans Allowance Act for a long time. But maybe when we come out of committee with the bill it will be better still. We shall do our best to see that it is, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed fortunate to follow such eminent speakers as the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I always feel that these two gentlemen are good spokesmen for veterans, and it is an honour to follow them.
The minister should certainly be congratulated on this legislation. Both previous speakers mentioned that, and I am in full agreement. This bill updates the existing act and brings it into modern times.
It is a long time since a lot of our veterans fought in the wars. It is 56 years since world war I, over 28 years since world war II, and 22 years since Korea. It is interesting that people in Canada and members of this House still want to be fair and, shall I say, generous to their veterans.
Some of our young people tend to make fun of those who were in the army or fought for their country in the last war. That is too bad, because they confuse the causes of war and the lack of vision of those who allowed war to

happen with the people who were compelled to fight for their country, either because of patriotism or because they were called up. Why they fought makes no difference. They went through two wars in some cases, and they fought for freedom. We must not forget that.
Last week, when I could not get a flight at the right hour, I came up by train and began reading the "Gulag Archipelago." I could not finish the book on the train and am still reading it. The big thing is that apparently after the First World War in mother Russia they sent those who had spoken in disparaging terms of the state into exile, after interrogation and torture, for perhaps one or two years, even though those exiled had not the slightest intention to incite revolution. In Canada that would never be allowed to happen.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) spoke about the good news and the bad news. He mentioned quarterly escalation of pensions. I agree with what he said. I do not see why it takes so long to escalate pensions. I really think we should try to make the computer work better. I know it has not worked too well for the UIC this past year, but it is working better. I hope it will turn out the cheques right on the date when the escalation in pensions should occur. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is to be congratulated for beginning this process. It applies to practically all pensions, and I do not see why we should not use it with veterans' pensions. They should be escalated every quarter, in line with the rise in the consumer price index, or whatever basis you use.
In the past, war veterans' legislation made little provision for children of veterans. That was very strange. The government increased family allowances for children up to $20 per child, and even this amount provides just a small amount of help. The point is this: the widow of a veteran with one child gets the same amount as the widow with two children. That is strange. The department and the board- and I congratulate Mr. Thompson-have decided that a flat rate of $50 is to be paid. The family allowance is deducted, so that if you get $20 in family allowance the flat rate under the veterans' legislation will be $30. I think this idea is sound.
My second point is that the bill will extend allowances for children up to age 25. This will allow the sons or daughters of veterans to continue their education without interruption. They will not need to leave school and work. That sort of thing delays graduation. I am glad that this provision has been introduced.
Another point which was covered by other members is that there is a flat rate or floor of $125 per month for the orphans of veterans. Previously, orphans were not well treated under the act. There is provision for up to three orphans of one family. Yet in some families there are five or six orphans. This, I think, should be examined.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said there is to be an increase in the ceiling of allowances paid to veterans and dependants. That ceiling will be escalated. I think this is very good.
Since we agree that we must treat our veterans generously, it is clear that, if we do not do these things provided
October 21, 1974

for in the bill, we shall treat our veterans shabbily. Mr. Speaker, the word to remember is shabby.
As other speakers said, the Veterans Land Act may be phased our next year. May I put in my oar in that respect. I ask the minister to consider helping veterans with housing. If this is in the works, I do not know. I think the veteran without money should be treated differently from the average citizen with little or no money. The advantage should always go to the veteran; he should get any differential.
I wish to make just one more point. The improvement in the escalation provided for in the bill is good. I feel that all veterans' pensions should be escalated, those paid to orphans as well as other pensions. Increasing the ceiling instead of paying the flat rate will be of great advantage. Only this way can we be generous to all veterans. Otherwise we shall treat them poorly.
I repeat, Canada owes a special debt to the men and women who served in times of crisis. I think this is a good bill, and support it fully. I hope the minister will consider the points I have mentioned. I commend him and the department for continued efforts to improve the lot of our veterans and their dependants.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the War Veterans Allowance Act became law in 1930 and was essentially designed as an old age pension for veterans who, because of the rigours of their service in the war theatres of World War I, were considered to have been pre-aged by about 10 years. Since then the act has been broadened to include veterans of the Nort-West Field Force, South African War, World II and Korean conflict, and their widows and orphans.
Bill C-4 contains a number of measures that the Progressive Conservative party has been seeking for some time now. We stated in our policy paper that we would introduce amendments to the War Veterans and Civilians Allowance Acts to ensure automatic increases bases on a three month cost of living index rather than on an annual basis. This would ensure more money for veterans more frequently.
The measure is most welcome, but we request an explanation of the reason quarterly increases were refused to orphans. This seems unjust. One can only hope it was merely an oversight.
The Progressive Conservative party advocates consultation with our provinces with a view to ensuring that increases in War Veterans Allowances do not lead to decreases in provincial social assistance payments. Has the government undertaken such consultations?
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), made mention of World War I veterans residing in the British Isles. I would also like to add my comments. At present there exists a restriction of 365 days' overseas service for veterans of World War I who enlisted prior to November 11, 1918. We suggest that this requirement be removed.
In order to receive an allowance outside Canada, a person must be a recipient at the time of his departure and
Veterans Affairs
must have resided in Canada for the 12 months immediately preceding the day he leaves Canada.
There are an estimated 10,000 Canadian veterans in the British Isles who have lived there since World War I or World War II. Many of these should be entitled to War Veterans Allowance, but have been unable to meet Canadian government regulations that demand that those who served in the forces spend at least one year in Canada before they can receive veterans allowance abroad.
There are many reasons why these veterans are not easily able to comply with these regulations. Some veterans are bed-ridden and paralyzed, eking out a precarious existence, and physically unable to come to Canada. Many are simply financially unable to make the long trip, with or without their families. Consequently there are some 600 or 700 Canadian veterans in great financial need in Britain alone.
There is no need for this situation to exist. Canada rightly looks after members of allied forces who are now in Canada; yet Canada ignores many of her own veterans who happen to be living abroad. I hope the minister will take note of my observations and take the necessary measures to bring in corrective legislation.

speechtext:
Who in this chamber is in a better position to make these comments than those who sit to the immediate left of the Speaker's chair?
I join my colleagues in supporting the passage of Bill C-4. It is especially fitting that we should be debating this bill and expediting its passage close to the eve of Remembrance Day, November 11. What better wreath could we place on the cenotaph to remember the dead of two world wars than this bill which gives benefit to the living veterans of those wars?
I congratulate the minister and his departmental officials on this bill. The remarks of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) indicated that we on this side of the House support these changes. We have advocated them, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe has made a real contribution to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He has made many positive suggestions to the department. He is respected by members of the committee, members on all sides of the House, and veterans from all across this land.
It is worth noting that members of the Standing Committee on Ve-.erans Affairs take a continuing non-partisan view of the problems of veterans. No other committee of

October 21, 1974
Veterans Affairs
this parliament has more good will or a more genuine desire to work for the benefit of those whom it is desirous of serving.
There is general agreement among all members of the House that this bill should be passed almost immediately. I have only two comments I wish to make. The first has to do with the increase in the income ceiling. According to this bill it is to be increased by a formula base which includes the consumer price index and other factors which have been detailed by previous speakers. However, due to the inflation which is rampant in today's economy, even with these increases the poor veteran will only find enough absolute dollars to pay his grocery bill. He will not be helped very much when it comes to the other costs such as shelter, heat, clothing and so on. While these increases are of some value to him, I do not feel they are overly generous.
Legislation introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) will make some changes to the Canada Pension Plan. The ceiling on income of people receiving the Canada Pension Plan will be completely removed for those over age 65. The Department of Veterans Affairs should take note of that precedent and introduce it as a regulation or, if necessary, as an amendment to the act. There is certainly a precedent. It would approach nearer to the guaranteed income spoken of by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I sincerely suggest this to the minister and his officials. I trust they will take due note of it.
Correspondence received by members of parliament concerns a number of problems affecting veterans. One problem that recurs quite often is the matter of over-payment of War Veterans Allowance, often that paid to the widow of a deceased veteran. This is through no fault of hers. She is ignorant because she does not understand the regulations. She takes the cheques which come to her in good faith. The War Veterans Allowance Board suddenly notices she is being overpaid. They ask for repayment, which is their right.
It is agreed the terms are most generous, but in cases brought to my attention even the most generous terms can be a great hardship. Is there not some way in which the department could write off such overpayments? These could be judged on the merits of each case. I believe there are cases where the demands for repayment are amply justified. However, there are other cases which, with a real sense of humanity and generosity on the part of the department, could and should be written off.
In conclusion, I should like to pay a tribute to Mr. Don Thompson of the War Veterans Allowance Board whose kindness and courtesy to myself and, I am sure, to all other hon. members who inquire about particular problems relating to our constituents, is deeply appreciated.
I am told that speeches to be immortal need not be eternal, Mr. Speaker. With this maxim in mind I shall conclude my remarks forthwith.

maintopic: STATUTE LAW (VETERANS AND CIVILIAN WAR ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENTS ACT, 1974 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ENTITLEMENT AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join those who have spoken before me in welcoming this bill. My remarks will be brief and I am

sure we can pass the bill on second reading by ten o'clock. We would in no way delay the passage of this measure. The provisions it contains have been a long time coming and they have been requested, I am sure, by members in all parties in the House.
From my conversations with veterans and representatives of veterans organizations I find that many veterans are finding it increasingly difficult to live on their pensions and allowances. Each year it becomes a little harder for them to cope with the cost of living or, shall I say, the cost of staying alive-perhaps if we used the latter phrase we should find it would not roll off, our tongues as easily as does "the cost of living".
The Veterans Affairs Standing Committee is one of the truly non-partisan committees. I was very pleased to play my part in the work of that committee. Each of its members is anxious to get a better deal for the veteran. We all feel the bill should go farther than it does. We all feel that veterans should not be obliged to beg to anyone. We all feel that they should live their lives with honour and dignity. If there is any group which deserves a special place in our society it is the veterans.
Most veterans' organizations continue to serve their communities year after year. Along with other service clubs they sponsor a variety of projects. Indeed it has been the hallmark of their generation to give to their country and to their community. In many cases they get very little in return.
The bill before us will go a long way toward removing many of the inequities facing veterans in Canada. I should like to see the 365 days' overseas service requirement affecting world war I veterans removed. Surely, the few hundred thousand world war I veterans left in Canada should get all we can give them. I am confident those among the world war I veterans who presently qualify, that is, those who served more than a year overseas, would not deny these benefits to their fellow veterans.
I should also like to see consideration given to the position of veterans who served Canada well during times of war but who did not return to Canada. Surely we can consider their situation. There are only a few thousand left and, if we find ourselves able to consider programs of aid to the less fortunate in other nations, surely we can look after those Canadians who served their country in time of war either as members of the Canadian forces or as civilians on war duty for Canada. Let us first look after our own.
We know that many of them are living in Europe, especially in Britain where they are experiencing economic problems. I believe we should amend this legislation to include persons who, for one reason or another, chose not to return to Canada after their war services.
I do not suppose one could find anywhere in our society a group of people more fiercely proud of their service to their country than the veterans.-1 am one of them and I am proud to stand with them whenever I can. It is a source of inspiration to me to see how resourceful most veterans are, and how well they cope with the problems of the day. The members of the Veterans Affairs Committee look forward to receiving this bill and will, no doubt, return it to the House with all dispatch so that the benefits con-
October 21, 1974

tained therein can be put into effect with all possible speed.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED PAYMENT OF PENSIONS TO PERSONS BETWEEN 60 AND 65 WHO ARE NO LONGER EMPLOYED
SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED PAYMENT OF PENSIONS TO PERSONS BETWEEN 60 AND 65 WHO ARE NO LONGER EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday October 17, as recorded in Hansard at page 471, I sought under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion having to do with the proposed legislation for the payment of old age pensions to persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who are spouses of persons over 65. To my surprise there was not unanimous approval-somebody said no. Accordingly, I had no option but to put the same matter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in the form of a question which is to be found on page 479 of Hansard for the same date. My question read as follows:
In view of the justifiable complaints of many persons between the ages of 60 and 65 against the unfairness of their not being included in the proposed legislation regarding pensions, and despite there not being unanimous consent to the motion I moved earlier, will the minister give consideration to reviewing the proposed legislation and make pensions available across the board to those who are out of the labour market?
That latter phrase might have been expanded, of course, to read:
-to persons across the board who are between 60 and 65 and who are out of the labour market?
In all of this, Your Honour, we are dealing with a promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)
Adjournment Debate
during the last election campaign, a promise which was repeated in the Speech from the Throne and indicated in the list of bills to come before this session of parliament. The bill in question is one which will make available to persons between 60 and 65 years of age who are spouses a pension under the Old Age Security Act provided, of course, that the other spouse is over 65 and drawing a pension, and provided that between the two of them they meet a certain means or income test. The Minister of National Health and Welfare in his reply the other day admitted that when this proposal was made it was brought forward as an interim measure.
I well remember that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made the promise during the election campaign he referred to the very types of individuals that I have mentioned-spinsters, widows, bachelors and widowers- as not being covered. I certainly got the impression from what I heard the Prime Minister say that he knew that in due course the payment of pensions at age 60 would have to be made more general, and that it would have to cover all persons in the age bracket of 60 to 65 who are in need.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare now says that the measure is an interim one in the sense that it is a forerunner of a guaranteed annual income for persons of all ages who may be in need. He talked the other day as well about the plan as being one that would solve the problem of two persons trying to live on one pension. That is fine, Mr. Speaker, but what about the one person trying to live on no pension?
It is all very fine to say to a married person, woman or man, who is between the age of 60 and 65, "Because your spouse is getting a pension we are going to give you one too". What about the single person, whether spinster, bachelor, widow or widower, who is in that same bracket, who is also in need, has no pension and is not to qualify under this legislation?
To my mind, no matter how much the minister tries to say that this is an interim measure in the way that he described it the other day, the fact is that in the eyes of the people and the country generally it is a pension payable at age 60; and there is going to be a very great feeling of unfairness when one 63 year old woman gets it because her husband is 66 and on a pension, and another 63 year old woman does not get it because she is a widow or a spinster. I could reverse the situation and speak of a 63 year old man under the same conditions.
I suggest that because of this unfairness that people are going to feel, the minister is starting off on the wrong foot by bringing in these pensions at 60 only in the case of the spouse between the ages of 60 and 65, rather than in the case of all those in that area who need it. I am quite prepared, as I have indicated in all of the speeches I have made on this matter over many years, to accept an employment test, to say that pensions are to be paid only to those persons between 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market. That will cover all the spouses who would meet the conditions of the minister's proposal, but it would be fairer, more general, and would not have the shortcomings that are in the minister's plan.

October 21, 1974
Adjournment Debate
When I tried the other day to move my motion under Standing Order 43, the Chair had something to say about there not being urgency to the question. There was no opportunity to argue it then and I am not now arguing with Mr. Speaker's ruling. But in my view the urgency of the matter is that once the minister's bill comes in it is pretty hard to get it changed.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED PAYMENT OF PENSIONS TO PERSONS BETWEEN 60 AND 65 WHO ARE NO LONGER EMPLOYED
speechtext:
The hon. member has a lot of explanations to give. In regard to his suggestion that the proposal put forward will bring unhappiness to the country, let me say I think it will bring unhappiness only if he goes around confusing the issue and trying to mislead the people as to the intention of this particular proposal. I am convinced that the hon. member is not a man who would intentionally mislead the people.
The purpose of this bill, which I repeat is an interim measure, is to make provision for a couple when one is forced to retire at age 65 and they find themselves living on the pension of one. The hon. member asks about the other situation where a single person is living at age 60

without a pension. I can only ask about such an individual who is 58 or 59.
I appeal to the hon. member to understand the general principle of a guaranteed income. I hope we will soon be in a position to come to the aid of people who are in need, whatever their ages. The idea that there will be some great solution to our social security problems in dishing out hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars to people between the ages of 60 and 65 including those who might not need it, is not realistic. That is not the way to come to the aid of needy people in our society.
I urge the hon. member that he really look at this proposal and see the purpose of it in the broader context of a general guaranteed income for all those in need, whatever the age or condition.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CERTAIN PENSION PROGRAMS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CERTAIN PENSION PROGRAMS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes I get a shock here. This is the second time I have been on my feet in one day. I sometimes wonder why I am not recognized during the question period, so thank God there is a late show once in a while.
The subject of my question is closely related to the matter dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). On October 15 I asked whether any consideration was being given, in consultation with the provinces, to increasing the national minimum of $75 a month in allowances for the blind and disabled. I appreciate the minister's answer as I know he is aware of the problem. He indicated his government was trying to do away with special categories by introducing a guaranteed annual income. I agree to some extent that this is a step in a desirable direction, but there are two categories of people, the blind and the disabled, who deserve immediate attention, perhaps even on an emergency basis, particularly as the increases in the cost of living have a greater effect on them than on the ordinary welfare recipient.
Surely it must be realized that those suffering exceptional incapacity deserve extra help because they suffer from adverse conditions? Surely the blind, the crippled, who under no circumstances can help themselves, in a great number of cases require some form of attendance, assistance, special nutritional foods, and so forth? Surely the bedridden and the permanent cripple who was born with defects cannot manage to exist under the strain of rampant inflation?
I believe these people are deserving of consideration. Surely the mentally retarded, the person suffering from cancer, or the person with a tumor are deserving of exceptional incapacity allowances even perhaps in cases where the husband or spouse is earning an income over the maximum allowable?
The Blind Persons Act an the Disabled Persons Act are under provincial aegis and it is their responsibility. Yet when I approach the provincial government I am told I should take up the matter with the Department of National Health and Welfare.
October 21, 1974

All of us would like to see a guaranteed annual income. I realize the difficulty the minister has in compiling all the various fixed income programs. It does not look as if we will have a guaranteed annual income in the very near future. If we are to await the result of the pilot project that is taking place in some areas under federal-provincial co-operation, these incapacitated people will continue to suffer. In the meantime what do the blind people do in order to cope with the increases in the cost of living? All I can say to the minister is that while I appreciate he is confronted with various problems, in the meantime an emergency situation exists in Canada in respect of these people who have been born with defects with which they cannot cope.
The bill that has been passed tonight in respect of the allowances for veterans will mean additional income. All I can do is appeal to the minister again to take the initiative. I realize the provinces are at fault. I even blame my own province where we have a government whose policies coincide with those of the official opposition. However, I hope that something can be done to help these people cope with the serious situation facing them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO CERTAIN PENSION PROGRAMS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) on this particular issue. The points he has indicated are quite correct particularly with regard to the province of Newfoundland which has elected to retain the Blind Persons Act. However, between the guaranteed annual income of the near future and the Blind and Disabled Persons Acts of the present there is another option available to the province. But it is up to the provincial government to take advantage of the Canada Assistance Plan. I should like to take a few minutes to clarify the situation.
As the hon. member knows, under the Canada Assistance Plan the granting of assistance is based on the need of an individual or family as determined by the province, rather than on the categorization which in the past limited assistance to those who were blind, disabled, aged or unemployed. This philosophy was formally embodied in the Canada Assistance Plan which was introduced in 1966. Through agreements with the provinces under this act, the federal government shares in the cost of providing financial assistance and welfare services to all persons who are in need for whatever reason.
Because of the limitations of the categorical programs which preceded the Canada Assistance Plan, it was decided that, effective 1981, the federal government would cease to participate in these programs, namely the Blind Persons and Disabled Persons Acts. Most provinces have in fact ceased to accept applications under these programs and have transferred recipients to their more comprehensive assistance program.
However, some blind and disabled persons could not qualify for the greater benefits available under the comprehensive program, primarily because their assets exceeded the allowable limits. Therefore, as of March 31, 1974, Manitoba and New Brunswick were still accepting applications under both the Blind and Disabled Persons Act, while Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland were only accepting them under the Blind Persons Act. At the end of the last fiscal year there were 1,814
Adjournment Debate
recipients of blind persons allowances and 4,369 of disabled persons allowances.
While it is true that allowances have not been increased recently under these programs, the mechanism by which applicants are assessed is less stringent than that under the Canada Assistance Plan. Therefore, recipients are usually allowed more assets, and federal payments such as family allowances and OAS/GIS are not counted as heavily in determining eligibility. I would also like to make clear that in those provinces where applications are still being accepted under the categorical programs, supplementary benefits under their assistance programs are available.
With the completion of the federal-provincial review of Canada's social security programs I am confident that problems such as those created by the categorization of assistance recipients can be resolved, as I indicated to the hon. member in the previous answer.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF REGIONAL WAGE DISPARITIES
PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF REGIONAL WAGE DISPARITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 11 I asked a question of the newly appointed President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) regarding his intention to work toward the phasing out of regional wage inequalities. I pointed out that this was a commitment made during the recent election campaign by some Liberal candidates in the Atlantic area.
I do not raise this matter in a spirit of sarcasm but merely to put on the record that, for example, Mr. Patterson, the candidate who ran against the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), was very emphatic about this. He is reported in the Halifax Herald in June as saying that he was winning support within the ranks of his party for his policy of wage parity for several workers in the area. He said that a motion to this effect was endorsed at a meeting of Atlantic Liberal candidates in Halifax, and he claimed that he had won the support of three cabinet ministers for equity and was putting the question to every cabinet minister who visited the area. Another candidate who ran unsuccessfully against a former deputy speaker of this House expressed similar sentiments in the press.
The cabinet of this administration, Mr. Speaker, has on some occasions expressed sympathy for the concept of working out ways to stop the practice of one department undoing what the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is trying to do.
In response to what I asked concerning his attitude toward the perpetuation of regional wage inequities, on October 15 in committee the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) said:
My own basic philosophy-and I do not like to evade the question- is that there has to be some consistency in government policy. When we apply minimum wages we apply them across the country. If you are going to reduce regional disparity, you are not going to reduce it by perpetuating-
The minister went on to say that he never believed the cost of living in Halifax, for example, was substantially lower than in central Canada.

October 21, 1974
Adjournment Debate
I would like to urge the President of the Treasury Board to make a policy commitment to work actively toward phasing out this practice of paying people under his employ less money in one part of the country for the same kind of work their brethren are doing in a different part of the country.
At the present time PSA negotiators are dealing with the Treasury Board on wage issues in the general category of labour and trades in the Atlantic region. In this context, it is necessary to quote from a letter written by the former president of the treasury board on July 16 this year in answer to an inquiry from my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, relating to the statements of Liberal candidates that I referred to earlier.
The then president of the treasury board in his letter of July 16, 1974, which I shall quote in part, said:
It is not desirable to create a general disparity between Public Service rates in lower-income areas and those paid by private industry and other levels of government. The provincial governments, on their part, are sensitive to federal Public Service rates of pay which are in excess of their rates.
From my knowledge, the trend is not that federal civil servants are paid more than their counterparts in provincial or private sector employment. In many cases it is the direct opposite. I refer to a situation which arose not many months ago involving nurses under federal jurisdiction, who were paid less than their sisters in the private sector and, in some cases, those working for the provinces.
In the Halifax area there is substantial differential in the pay of certain trades. Boilermakers employed federally made approximately $2.63 an hour less than their counterparts in provincial or private employment. Electricians make approximately $2.44 an hour less and labourers $2.12 less, even when one takes into account fringe benefits which have been made available to those employed in the federal public service and not available to those employed in the private or provincial sector.
I suggest that not one premier of Canada actively supports the type of wage policy espoused by Treasure Board at this time. I know that it is impractical to end regional pay differences in one fell swoop. As an interim measure it should be possible to achieve parity with the best paid people in a region. I believe the PSA is adopting a policy of designating areas within so-called depressed regions. For example, in Nova Scotia it would be Halifax, and in Quebec, Montreal and so on.
In those areas the standard of wages could be determined and Treasury Board could make sure that a wage equivalent to that paid in other sectors is paid to those in federal employ, even if one takes into account fringe
benefits. The PSA, as an interim measure, wants wage equality in the different regions of the country.
I hope the President of the Treasury Board adopts the philosophical attitude which was shown recently by the Postmaster General in committee. Let him assure us that in future he will end the practice which runs counter, as the Postmaster General among others said, to the aims in the various regions, of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF REGIONAL WAGE DISPARITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without doubt there are clearly identifiable regional labour and pay markets in Canada for certain occupations. The hon. member alluded, I think, to the possibility of setting up pilot projects in places like Halifax and Montreal, under which rates of pay could be set.
Rates of pay, pay systems, and administrative rules governing pay in that part of the federal public service for which the Treasury Board is the employer, are items that are subject to negotiation under the Public Service Staff Relations Act. That we must bear in mind. Consequently, changes in pay systems cannot be made unilaterally by the government as employer. Any modifications of present regional rate systems and the extension of regional pay systems to other occupational groups can only flow from agreements between the government as employer and the bargaining agent, or from awards rendered by the arbitration tribunal.
It is the policy of the government as employer to try to bargain regional rates with certified bargaining agents where it is feasible and appropriate to do so; that is, for those groups where public servants are located in two or more regions of Canada, where the pay data for similar occupational groups in the private sector indicate significant regional variations from the Canadian average, and where the area of recruitment and the mobility of employees within the public service are limited.
These circumstances are typically found in groups in the operational category and the administrative support category, but they exist in groups in other categories as well. Paying national rates of pay in such circumstances can only result in some public servants receiving less than their counterparts in their region and others receiving rates in excess of those prevailing in their particular region.
To adopt a simplistic approach, paying one rate for right across Canada, in essence begs the question, begs the reality.
